title: Do Companies Deliver on Their IPO Claims?
abstract: Initial public offering (IPO) filings describe what a company does and what it intends to become. Yet whether individual forward-looking claims are subsequently realized is difficult to assess. We introduce Vision Follow-Through (VFT), a benchmark and agentic pipeline that separates claim extraction, category assignment, verifiability, and evidence-grounded follow-through assessment. \vftclaims{} contains 5,066 human-annotated claim spans from 50 IPO filings, while \vftverify{} adds verifiability tiers, follow-through outcomes, and cited later evidence for 1,000 claims. Across language models, classifying human-annotated claims is substantially easier than extracting claims from full filings. Extraction coverage also varies sharply by category, with Organizational/Culture claims recovered far less often than Market Opportunity claims. Follow-through assessment poses a separate challenge: model judgments diverge from human assessments in different ways rather than exhibiting a single consistent bias. These results show that reliable assessment of corporate follow-through requires both finding the relevant claims and grounding subsequent judgments in later evidence.

title: Weight-space programming and mechanistic interpretability for model editing in particle physics
abstract: We demonstrate that weight-space programming and edits guided by sparse autoencoders can remove unwanted aspects of a particle-physics foundation model through direct edits to its weights. In a foundation model trained on jets, we observe that adding a single soft neutral particle causes large changes in jet classification, violating infrared safety. We locate the responsible attention heads with mechanistic analysis and trace the flaw's origin to pretraining on datasets with different reconstruction thresholds. We then propose two targeted approaches to repair the flaw: by removing three latent directions identified with sparse autoencoders, and by letting language-model agents edit the weights directly, without gradients and with only 50 queries to the model. Both their edits individually remove almost the entire flaw and leave the rest of the model's response nearly unchanged. Compared to fine-tuning, both methods change far fewer parameters. Although built only on $W$ and QCD jets, the edits carry over to all signal classes, the pretrained generator, and a newly trained regression head.

title: Multimodal AI fusion for colorectal cancer survival prediction
abstract: This research poster presents a multimodal deep learning study for predicting overall survival in colorectal cancer. The study uses patient-matched whole-slide images (WSIs), structured clinical data, and survival outcomes from the MCO (1,375 patients) and TCGA (555 patients) cohorts, with a 59-month analysis horizon. The study compares WSI-only models, a tabular FT-Transformer, and a multimodal hypergraph that uses cross-attention to incorporate clinical features into the image representation. Models were assessed using the concordance index (C-index) through patient-level cross-validation within each cohort and external validation in both directions. The multimodal hypergraph outperformed all WSI-only models across the four validation settings. When pathology and staging variables were excluded, it also outperformed the tabular model in both external validations. The FT-Transformer with all variables achieved the highest mean C-index in every setting (0.715–0.766). Future work will investigate which tissue features provide complementary prognostic information and develop an agentic AI layer to support model selection, hyperparameter exploration, experiment tracking, and comparison of fusion strategies.

title: Cross-Site Transformers Are Robust Heart Rate Estimators
abstract: Single-site heart-rate estimation from photoplethysmography (PPG) degrades sharply under real-world motion. Multi-site PPG provides a natural solution, but existing models fuse sites as generic sensor channels rather than exploiting their hemodynamic structure: each heartbeat propagates along the arterial tree, appearing across body sites as delayed and transformed copies of the same cardiac event. We propose the Cross-Site Transformer, which introduces a hemodynamically informed inductive bias by restricting multi-sensor fusion to cross-attention between PPG sites. On WildPPG, the largest in-the-wild benchmark available, our model establishes a new single-model state of the art, reducing error by 21% over the previous best and 35% over the best prior transformer. The same cross-site restriction makes the trained network directly auditable. Because each cross-attention head lies on one directed pathway between sites, causal resample ablation can isolate and test each direction of information flow. Ablating the chest-to-wrist pathway doubles error, whereas the reverse costs far less. Encoding hemodynamic structure into attention routing thus improves real-world sensing robustness and enables rigorous auditing of multi-sensor fusion.

title: Graph Signal Generation via Graph-Aware Diffusion Models
abstract: Many signals are defined on the nodes of a graph, such as traffic flow at road sensors or user purchases of related products. They are often partly observed, and learning their distribution enables imputing missing values and forecasting future ones. Diffusion models learn such distributions, but their forward noise is independent across nodes and does not depend on the graph. We introduce graph-aware diffusion (GAD), whose forward process is a heat diffusion on the graph driven by Gaussian noise. In the graph Fourier basis, the forward transition is a scalar Gaussian channel at each frequency. With a shared diffusion rate, high graph frequencies are attenuated faster than low ones. We propose Mode-Adaptive SNR Scheduling (MASS), which assigns each graph frequency its own diffusion rate and keeps all of them at the same SNR. For graph-stationary signals, MASS equalizes the normalized error of the optimal linear denoiser across frequencies. We bound reverse-SDE stiffness as a function of the (shifted) Laplacian's condition number, with a logarithmic upper bound for MASS and a linear lower bound for shared rates. GAD with MASS improves recommendation accuracy by 5-19%, reduces traffic-imputation RMSE by up to 7.8% with half as many reverse steps, and improves forecasting MAE and RMSE using only 3 reverse steps.

title: Error-Corrected Physics-Informed Neural Operator for Optimal Control of Unmanned Aerial Vehicles under Uncertainty
abstract: We solve open-loop optimal control problems under parametric uncertainty using a physics-informed DeepONet that returns trajectories for all sampled scenarios in one evaluation. Trained only on the residual at generic controls, the operator is reused across targets and horizons. Because a gradient-based optimizer exploits surrogate errors, we correct the prediction by one Newton step on the dynamics, computed for all scenarios and times by one parallel scan. The corrected state has a second-order error bounded by the residual alone, and the corrected cost is honest for every control up to the sampling error. On a fixed-wing UAV benchmark, the corrected operator matches the accuracy of a batched Adam solver and an Ipopt solver at equal sample size and is 8 times faster than the Adam solver on the same GPU at a few hundred scenarios and 15 times faster than Ipopt on a CPU.

The corrected state has a second-order error bounded by the residual alone, and the corrected cost is honest for every control up to the sampling error. On a fixed-wing UAV benchmark, the corrected operator matches the accuracy of a batched Adam solver and an Ipopt solver at equal sample size and is 8 times faster than the Adam solver on the same GPU at a few hundred scenarios and 15 times faster than Ipopt on a CPU.

title: Accelerating Muon with Spectral Residual Correction
abstract: Muon constructs matrix updates by applying a matrix-sign transformation to momentum. A common route to accelerating Muon is to modify the gradient or momentum before this transformation. We explore a complementary direction: refining the parameter step while retaining Muon's momentum recursion. Derived from the parameter subproblem of the ADMM-Inspired Momentum framework, AIMuon uses the gradient--momentum residual to correct the tentative spectral step. The residual undergoes a separate matrix-sign transformation, while spectral--nuclear duality determines the relative weighting of the momentum and residual directions. In practice, both directions are approximated with Newton--Schulz iterations and their combination is rescaled to match Muon's update magnitude. We establish a stochastic stationarity bound for the corresponding exact iteration. On GPT-2-small, GPT-2-medium, and Qwen3-0.6B, AIMuon reaches Muon's final validation loss with 8.98\%, 10.05\%, and 6.49\% fewer optimization steps, respectively, while achieving lower final validation loss than Muon, Muon-Nesterov, and MONA.

title: Contrastive On-Policy Distillation via Dual-Branch Supervision
abstract: For on-policy distillation (OPD), more capable models are a natural choice as teachers. However, higher task performance does not necessarily imply greater teachability. A controlled token intervention study suggests that even a model weaker than the student can serve as an informative contrastive reference. Building on this observation, we propose Contrastive On-Policy Distillation (cOPD), which provides dual branch supervision by contrasting strong teacher, weak teacher, and student predictions at student generated prefixes. Our analysis explains how this three way comparison helps select token candidates associated with better or worse reasoning outcomes under an idealized model. We evaluate cOPD across diverse teacher student configurations spanning different training stages, parameter scales, and model families, on tasks including mathematical reasoning, instruction following, and question answering with abstention. cOPD achieves the best or top-tier performance among the evaluated baselines across all three tasks, improving overall Pass@16 on mathematical reasoning by up to 7.51\% over the strongest baseline. Further analyses show that cOPD suppresses undesirable response patterns and suggest that it facilitates exploration.

title: The Value of Labels in Data Selection for Least Squares
abstract: Suppose a selector sees a finite labelled dataset and chooses $n$ of its rows, with repetition. Ordinary least squares is then fitted to the rows that were chosen, without weights, and the excess loss of the fit on the full dataset is measured in units of the optimal loss. Without further assumptions this ratio does not decay with $n$. We examine the problem for $d$ features and rows of normalized leverage at most $κ$, and determine or bound the leading constants. A selector that must establish its rule before seeing the labels has an optimal worst-case ratio of $dκ/n$ to leading order, whatever use it makes of the features. With scalar labels, a selector that sees the labels achieves a value between $dκ/(2n)$ and $dκΛ_d/n$, where $Λ_d<1$ is the rounding constant of mean selection. For $d\le4$, the constant is then $dκ/2$, so that labels are worth exactly a factor of two there, and for one feature and $m$ outputs it is $κΛ_m$. With two or more features the selector can change the proportions of the frequent rows and therefore reshape its own design matrix. We design a simplified optimization problem, which we call a game, that bounds the constant for datasets with exactly fitted frequent rows, then show that its value is at most one half of the gradient energy in several regimes, and that one half is exact along directions in which the frequent rows are rigid, such as an intercept. For grouped designs, in which reshaping amounts to the allocation of a common budget, the constant is $27d/128$ up to an additive constant, compared with $d$ without labels. Nevertheless, one half is not the constant in every dimension: we construct datasets of extremely high dimension and large leverage on which every selection has an excess ratio of at least $(e^{-1/2}-o(1))\,dκ/n$, so that labels are worth at most a factor close to $\sqrt e$ there.

title: Mixture of Latent Recursions for Low-Rank Adaptation
abstract: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) performs task-specific adaptation using a fixed low-rank architecture, whose expressiveness is typically increased by enlarging or adding learnable modules with a proportional parameter overhead. We introduce Mixture of Latent Recursions (MoLR), an adaptive recursion framework that enhances adaptation expressiveness while preserving parameter efficiency. MoLR recursively refines the down-projected latent representation of each input using a shared transformation. A lightweight threshold-based router independently determines whether each token should undergo further refinement, while dynamically adjusted thresholds encourage balanced utilization across recursion depths. Extensive experiments across diverse language and vision tasks demonstrate that MoLR consistently outperforms representative LoRA variants with negligible parameter overhead over LoRA. Further analyses show that MoLR learns input-dependent recursion-depth allocation and enables a controllable inference-time compute-performance trade-off without requiring retraining. Code will be publicly available.

title: PhiJEPA: Denoising Latent Predictions for Visual Representation Learning
abstract: Can a predictor trained to infer hidden image regions still help a world model plan when part of an object disappears from view and the visible context is blurred? We introduce PhiJEPA, a joint-embedding predictive architecture that adapts PhiNet's two-stage prediction to masked Transformers. From sparse, photometrically corrupted context, a Transformer block predicts hidden tokens of an independently corrupted teacher view. A token-wise MLP then maps these predictions to clean teacher tokens. Controlled ablations show that the combined objective improves dense features over the tested one-stage alternatives. Pre-trained on ImageNet-1K with $5.6\times10^{19}$ training FLOPs, PhiJEPA achieves 69.3 mIoU on linear PASCAL VOC segmentation, exceeding the evaluated I-JEPA and DSeq-JEPA checkpoints in segmentation accuracy, with 25\% fewer training FLOPs than I-JEPA. It also improves hidden-region segmentation over Simple I-JEPA (49.1 vs.\ 44.3 mIoU). As an application, we use the frozen encoder in DINO-WM on PushT, and reuse the pre-training predictor, which JEPAs usually discard, to complete occluded tokens without fine-tuning. In open-loop planning with simultaneous object occlusion and Gaussian blur ($σ=2$ pixels), predictor completion raises success from 33\% to 65\%, compared with 25\% for Simple I-JEPA with its predictor and 40\% for iBOT with pixel inpainting. Together, these results support two-stage latent prediction as an efficient approach to learning visual representations that remain useful under photometric degradation and support completion under partial observation.

title: MODULE: A Mutual-Promoting Deep Unfolding Framework Towards Degradation-Robust Multi-modal Image Fusion
abstract: Multi-modal image fusion is crucial for comprehensive scene representation, yet real-world degradations compromise its efficacy, necessitating degradation-robust fusion paradigms. Existing degradation-robust multi-modal image fusion methods are often hindered by cascaded sub-optimal solution or black-box opacity. To address these challenges, we propose a theory-inspired mutual-promoting deep unfolding framework. It reformulates degradation-robust image fusion as a joint optimization problem, utilizing the degradation model and modality generation mechanism to explicitly model both single-task priors and cross-task dependencies. By decomposing the complex multi-task optimization problem into task-related iterative subproblems, the framework establishes a bidirectional reciprocal information flow between restoration and fusion. This process is further unfolded into a multi-stage deep neural network, where each component explicitly corresponds to a specific mathematical operation. In our framework, the fused cross-modal prior actively regularizes the ill-posed restoration, while the purified modality features continuously refine the fusion output. It ensures a transparent architecture that combines the merits of both model-based and data-driven methodologies. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our paradigm achieves state-of-the-art performance while providing superior interpretability. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/Meskend/MODULE.

title: Anomaly Detection in Time Series with Enhanced Privacy Using Self-Supervised Contrastive Learning
abstract: Anomaly detection in time series is increasingly used for sensitive data, including medical and physiological data. However, these data carry a substantial risk of information leakage, making privacy preservation through anonymization essential. While anonymization reduces the risk of privacy breach, it can also remove informative features, creating a trade-off between privacy preservation and anomaly-detection performance. To address this challenge, we propose a robust framework that mitigates this trade-off and enables high-accuracy anomaly detection on anonymized data. Our approach centers on an anonymization function that transforms a time series by removing sensitive information, including contextual features and personally identifiable information, while retaining information that is beneficial for anomaly detection. We introduced a privacy model that guides the training of the anonymization function and optimizes the two components in an adversarial manner using contrastive loss in opposite directions. This design uses the anonymization function to eliminate sensitive information captured by the privacy model. We incorporate an anomaly detection loss function to ensure that the anonymization function preserves the essential information required for accurate anomaly detection. The effectiveness of the anonymization process and its impact on anomaly-detection performance were evaluated using multiple real-world and synthetic datasets. Results showed that our method reduced privacy-related information leakage by 42.65% while incurring only a 2.58% decrease in the F1 score for anomaly detection.

title: Engram: Multi-Stage Memory for Agentic Tuning of Heterogeneous Models
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can now tune neural networks, yet without cross-session memory they spend costly trials rediscovering known lessons. Reuse is difficult because production models differ in architecture, training setup and inference budget. We present Engram, a memory system that links past trial outcomes with the hypotheses and rationale behind them and assesses whether this evidence applies to the current model. An online agent curates evidence at the decision points where it is needed: Initial Guidance supplies validated lessons at the start, Session Retrieval supplies related past sessions before each batch of hypotheses is generated, and Trial Candidate Review checks each trial candidate against matching past trials. Between sessions, an offline agent distills validated lessons, making the memory self-improving. On two ads models, Engram reaches the 32-trial result of a no-memory control with 47% fewer trials and also ends with a better model on average.

title: Underwater Spectral Recovery via Multi-View Hyperspectral Imaging
abstract: Underwater imaging suffers from wavelength-dependent absorption and scattering that distort scenes and obscure spectral signatures. While RGB restoration improves visual clarity, the outputs remain broadband and tied to the sensor's color space. We introduce a physically grounded framework that lifts underwater restoration to continuous spectral radiance using multi-view hyperspectral imaging. By representing continuous spectra via low-rank basis functions and leveraging multi-distance observations, our framework jointly constrains scene radiance and water parameters. We employ a robust sparse-to-dense pipeline: water parameters are estimated from consistent multi-view matches and then applied globally to invert the light transport model across the full images. Validated on physics-based synthetic data rendered via the Mitsuba 3 spectral path tracer, our method recovers physically meaningful radiance spectra and, as a downstream application, outperforms standard image restoration baselines.

title: Beyond a Single Human Demonstration: Learning from Scored Trajectory Alternatives for End-to-End Driving
abstract: Human driving logs record only one trajectory per scene, leaving other feasible driving choices without explicit trajectory targets or quality labels. This limits supervision for end-to-end planners that generate and refine multiple candidate trajectories. Meanwhile, conditioning refinement on a large vision-language model adds substantial online inference cost. We propose DriveSTA, which extends autoregressive proposal generation and proposal-conditioned residual flow refinement with scored trajectory alternatives. For each training scene, we generate alternatives offline through smooth deformations of the recorded trajectory and evaluate their simulated execution against logged traffic. Diverse, high-quality alternatives supervise distinct proposals and define residual targets for quality-guided denoising, while candidates spanning the full score range train a scorer to assess driving quality. A shared joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA), adapted through masked video-feature prediction, encodes observed frames once and provides temporal context for both refinement and scoring. On NAVSIM v1 Navtest, DriveSTA ranks first among the compared planners trained on NAVSIM data alone. With expanded training data, DriveSTA-Scale achieves state-of-the-art results among the compared methods on Navtest and closed-loop HUGSIM, while reducing mean planner forward-pass latency by 73% relative to ChainFlow-VLA in matched evaluations.

title: Budgeted Safety Verification for Streaming Video Generation
abstract: A streamed video generator releases each chunk the moment that it is produced, so a safety decision that waits for the finished clip arrives after the harm has been seen. We measure a guardrail by exposure, the harmful frames a viewer is shown, and ask where a fixed moderation budget should be spent. The accurate detector reads decoded frames with a video language model and is too expensive for every chunk, so our guard reads hidden states the generator has computed already and spends a cheap score on deciding when to call it. On 599 streams from a distilled causal generator the undefended model shows 46.25 harmful frames of 81. The video model on every chunk leaves 0.91 frames at 80.1 scored per benign stream, and the same model triggered by our guard leaves 2.35 at 5.3. Spending that budget at random leaves 37.20 frames, so the gain is in the ordering, and a frame detector in the same role gives up almost six, so the judging stage must read the chunk as a clip. The ordering is worth more as the stream lengthens, and the guard carries to a second system. An independent guardrail model agrees with our oracle at $κ=0.74$, and a blinded audit by 50 participants puts its precision at 96.1% and recall at 82.8%. Warning. This paper contains examples of generated content that some readers may find disturbing or offensive in nature.

title: When Do LLM-Elicited Priors Help? A Controlled Audit of Language Models as Priors for Small-Sample Bayesian Regression
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly asked where to center the coefficients of a small-sample Bayesian regression, but the evidence is unclear: benchmarks are often built to match the prior and models may remember them. We audit this practice with one frontier and one flash-tier model, using hidden feature names, post-cutoff housing data and a pre-specified test that gives features the wrong descriptions. First, the models share their errors (correlation $0.92$--$0.99$ across draws, vendors and paraphrases): averaging $20$ draws is no more accurate than one, and treating draws as independent creates overconfidence. Much of this error comes from reporting each feature's effect alone, not with the others held fixed. Second, against the best classical prior, the LLM center helps clearly on one of four benchmarks (RMSE $-5.8\%$), marginally on two, and hurts mean RMSE on the fourth. Third, the LLM's stated uncertainty is unreliable; letting the data set the prior scale cuts the harm of a wrong center four-fold against a unit-variance prior. A pre-specified external test returned the verdict \textsc{partial}: on $18$ rule-selected problems the center helps on six and hurts on four, and a hard trust gate trusts a harmful prior while an evidence-weighted mixture is safer.

title: Self-Reported State Empathy in Response to Video Stimuli: Comparing the Measurement Characteristics of Cognitive and Affective Empathy
abstract: In this study, we propose an 8-item self-reported state empathy scale comprising four cognitive empathy (CE) and four affective empathy (AE) items to evaluate empathic responses to video stimuli on a per-trial basis and examine its measurement characteristics. For a scale to function as a state measurement, its scores must fluctuate according to the nature of the presented scene, rather than only with stable between-participant differences. Therefore, we had 10 participants repeatedly respond to 24 video stimuli and decomposed the variation in the resulting 240 trials into stimulus effects, participant effects, and residuals. We further conducted correlation analyses using the inclusion of other in the self (IOS) scale and emotion congruence as external criteria for AE and video accuracy rate as an external criterion for CE. In the AE subscale, 42.8% of the variance was attributed to stimulus effects and 8.9% to participant effects, and AE correlated positively with the IOS ( r =.772) and emotion congruence ( r =.308). Conversely, in the CE subscale, the participant effect (33.9%) exceeded the stimulus effect (12.0%), no positive correlation with the video accuracy rate was found, and the CE scores remained high even in incorrect emotion recognition trials. These results suggest that AE captures affective empathic responses that vary with video stimuli, whereas CE, whose internal consistency was low (α=.581), tends to reflect a subjective sense of understanding rather than objective recognition accuracy; the CE results should therefore be interpreted with caution. This study clarified the different measurement characteristics of self-reported CE and AE in state empathy measurement.

In the AE subscale, 42.8% of the variance was attributed to stimulus effects and 8.9% to participant effects, and AE correlated positively with the IOS ( r =.772) and emotion congruence ( r =.308). Conversely, in the CE subscale, the participant effect (33.9%) exceeded the stimulus effect (12.0%), no positive correlation with the video accuracy rate was found, and the CE scores remained high even in incorrect emotion recognition trials. These results suggest that AE captures affective empathic responses that vary with video stimuli, whereas CE, whose internal consistency was low (α=.581), tends to reflect a subjective sense of understanding rather than objective recognition accuracy; the CE results should therefore be interpreted with caution. This study clarified the different measurement characteristics of self-reported CE and AE in state empathy measurement.

title: Real-time event-level zero-shot learning at 150 ns: towards a foundation model for particle physics experiment triggering
abstract: The hardware-based Level-1 triggers of the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) experiments select collisions with algorithms designed for one signature each, acting on a coarse, low-latency view of every event. We present a learned event embedding for several trigger tasks and evaluate its transfer to processes absent from training. Using paired offline and Level-1 views of the same simulated collisions, we train an offline transformer with a supervised metric loss and distil it, event by event, into a quantised Level-1 transformer whose bit widths are learned under a fixed resource budget. Trained on 25 Standard Model processes, the embedding places 28 held-out processes next to their physical relatives. A nearest-neighbour selection against background collisions, which never enter encoder training, rejects 99% of them. It retains a median of 90% of seen and 96% of unseen Standard Model events and 88% of a set of 52 beyond-the-Standard-Model benchmark samples, the best-performing score across the three groups among the baselines evaluated on the same events. A second gate against the seen processes isolates high-mass dilepton signals into label-free clusters, and long-lived signals too when displaced-track information is available. With 7512 parameters and an FPGA latency of 147 ns, the encoder uses one event representation, learned once, to derive several selections, opening the door to a foundation model for the LHC's hardware-based triggers.

title: Sampling non-abelian lattice gauge theories with diffusion models
abstract: We present gauge-equivariant diffusion models as samplers for lattice gauge theories (LGTs). Using lattice gauge-equivariant convolutional neural networks (L-CNNs) and the Metropolis-adjusted annealed Langevin algorithm (MAALA), we are able to accurately sample two-dimensional U(2) field configurations and show first promising results for four-dimensional SU(3). Our two-dimensional models extrapolate remarkably well to larger inverse couplings than originally trained on. We confirm this by comparing observables to analytically known values and to hybrid Monte Carlo results.

title: Deep Cross-Division Network for Product-and-Ratio Feature Interactions in Industrial Ranking
abstract: Learning effective feature interactions is essential for industrial recommender systems. DCN and DCNv2 efficiently automate polynomial feature crossing. However, their cross layers construct interactions using only non-negative integer powers of the input features, with the maximum degree controlled by network depth. Consequently, they cannot directly represent the reciprocal terms required for ratios, rates, and normalized counts unless such features are explicitly provided as inputs. We introduce DCDN, a Deep Cross-Division Network that augments a DCNv2-style cross layer with a division branch. DCDN jointly learns product, ratio, and mixed product-ratio interactions. We characterize the representable interactions as multivariate Laurent polynomials and show that a $K$-layer DCDN generates Laurent monomials of $\ell_1$-order up to $K+1$, with signed degree between $-K$ and $K+1$. We evaluate DCDN against a production-optimized neural-ranking baseline built around DCNv2 and supplied with manually engineered ratio features. Replacing the DCNv2 block with DCDN allowed us to eliminate the entire class of manually engineered ratio features from the model input, reducing the number of input features by $40.1\%$. DCDN is deployed in the production ranking stack of a major short-video service. In a live A/B test on this service, DCDN increased likes by $3.25\%$, shares by $16.26\%$, total view time (TVT) by $0.33\%$, and clicks to open fullscreen by $0.38\%$; all changes were statistically significant. The number of shown videos decreased slightly ($-0.24\%$). These results demonstrate that DCDN can improve user engagement while eliminating reliance on manually engineered ratio features. Our code is publicly released at https://github.com/rw404/DCDN.

title: PP-CFG: Polarity-Preserving Guidance for Controllable Few-Step Image and Video Generation
abstract: Few-step diffusion distillation reduces sampling cost but often weakens adjustable classifier-free guidance (CFG) and runtime negative prompting. We introduce PP-CFG, an architecture that keeps positive and negative text conditions separate and combines their attention responses with opposite signs within a shared visual backbone. Its Scale-Time Polarity Mixer refines each condition using the guidance scale and denoising timestep, allowing prompt influence to vary throughout generation. The student retains a continuous scale input and selectable negative prompts with one visual backbone pass per step. We evaluate PP-CFG on Wan2.1 for video generation with distribution matching distillation (DMD), and on Qwen-Image with both latent consistency model (LCM) distillation and DMD. PP-CFG achieves 81.46 VBench in four steps and lower video teacher-student distances across guidance scales than step-distilled DMD. On NegElement-1K, our benchmark of 1,000 matched image and video prompt cases, it achieves higher target-removal rates than the corresponding teachers. These experiments support the method's generality across attention architectures, generation modalities, and distillation objectives while retaining competitive generation quality.

title: Hindsight Forcing: Learning Better History from the Future in Autoregressive Video Diffusion
abstract: Few-step autoregressive video diffusion enables real-time streaming generation, with each generated chunk serving as historical context for subsequent generation. To avoid the memory explosion of backpropagation through time, previous self-rollout methods typically truncate cross-chunk gradients or detach historical latents. As a result, earlier denoising computations receive no downstream feedback through the generated history on how to synthesize frames that facilitate subsequent generation, leading to visual drift and structural collapse as rollouts extend. To address this limitation, we propose Hindsight Forcing, which allows historical chunks to learn directly from future outcomes by decoupling forward generation from backward credit assignment via a latent straight-through bridge. In the forward pass, each chunk completes a full multi-step rollout to update the KV cache. In the backward pass, the bridge routes gradients from future losses back to a single selected denoising step per historical chunk, training both the context writer and historical denoiser on shared parameters without retaining the full trajectory graph. Remarkably, Hindsight Forcing requires no additional model parameters, architecture modifications, or separate trajectory replay. Extensive experiments on VBench demonstrate that Hindsight Forcing outperforms existing baselines in overall visual quality and dynamic motion, while ablation studies validate the benefit of supervising historical denoising. Code is available at https://github.com/haonanAN309/Hindsight-Forcing.

title: State-Vector Simulation of 36-Qubit Ekerå–Håstad Factoring Using FP8 Storage on Commodity NVIDIA GB10 Hardware
abstract: We report an exact state-vector simulation of the semiclassically folded Ekerå–Håstad (EH) short discrete-logarithm factoring circuit up to 36 logical qubits on commodity NVIDIA GB10 unified-memory hardware (121 GiB per node). Pairing IEEE FP8 (e4m3, 2 bytes per complex amplitude) state-vector storage with FP32/FP64 arithmetic kernels and host-side double-precision global scale tracking enables factoring 35-bit balanced RSA semiprimes on two GB10 nodes (242 GiB aggregate memory), while the same single-node architecture (np = 1, without MPI) scales to 35 logical qubits on a single GB10 or proportionally on discrete-VRAM commodity GPUs. Over 100 GbE RoCE (HPCX OpenMPI + UCX rc), the verified 36-qubit factorization of N = 24,966,154,091 = 157007 x 159013 completes its successful 53-round run in 1,339.8 s (2,688.7 s across two attempts). Both the folded EH circuit and 2-byte/amplitude rescaled storage follow established prior art (Ekerå; De Raedt et al., JUQCS-A); this technical note serves as an open-access defensive publication and engineering benchmark. Both English and Chinese PDF editions are included.

title: Understanding Membership Inference Attacks on EEG Models
abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) signals contain sensitive, subject-specific information, making models trained on them potential targets for membership inference attacks (MIAs). Although MIAs have been studied extensively in other domains, their applications to EEG models are relatively scarce, and the factors driving the vulnerability of EEG models to MIAs are not adequately understood. In this paper, we present a systematic empirical analysis of MIAs on EEG models using three datasets, seven model architectures, four attack methods, and two metrics. Results show that poor model generalization (large train-test loss and accuracy gap) is the strongest indicator of MIA vulnerability. Longer training and larger models also increase vulnerability. Moreover, no particular scalp region, frequency band, inter-channel correlation pattern, or temporal versus spectral representation of EEG data consistently explains MIA vulnerability across datasets. Finally, subject identification and leave-one-subject-out experiments indicate that models relying more heavily on subject-specific representations are more vulnerable to MIAs. Overall, our findings identify the key drivers of membership leakage in EEG models and can provide guidance for developing MIA-resilient EEG systems.

title: Autonomous quantum machine learning via Riemannian gradient-based optimization
abstract: Quantum machine learning models typically rely on repeated quantum measurements and classical optimization during training, making the quantum-to-classical information-extraction process a fundamental bottleneck for scalability. We propose a framework for autonomous self-training quantum machine learning, based on Riemannian gradient optimization, in which the optimization proceeds entirely within the quantum domain without requiring quantum measurements or classical feedback. We derive the Riemannian gradient update rules for a broad class of learning tasks and identify sufficient conditions under which the resulting training dynamics can be realized fully autonomously. Within this regime, we establish an exponential convergence guarantee, in the training iterations, for sufficiently small step sizes, and further analyze the training cost in terms of the growth of the circuit depth. Importantly, we further show that the trained model can automatically discover symmetries hidden in the training data without $\textit{a priori}$ specification. For the canonical examples of quantum phase classification and unitary learning with a hidden symmetry, our numerical study indicates that learning can be achieved at low circuit depths with only a few distinct training examples. Our results thus establish autonomous quantum machine learning as a promising paradigm that removes the classical optimization loop while retaining strong theoretical guarantees and practical performances.

title: PGS-PCQA: Perceptually Gated Synthetic Supervision for No-Reference Point Cloud Quality Assessment
abstract: Existing no-reference point cloud quality assessment (NR-PCQA) methods perform well within individual datasets but generalize poorly across datasets. We identify insufficient distortion coverage in training data as a key cause: on unseen distortion types, models rank severity levels near chance or even in reverse. We propose perceptually gated synthetic supervision for no-reference point cloud quality assessment (PGS-PCQA), an NR-PCQA model trained with synthetic distortion ranking. It builds a synthetic distortion bank from source reference point clouds and uses within-type severity ranking as supervision in addition to the source mean opinion scores (MOS), requiring no subjective scores for the synthetic samples. Since higher severity does not always mean lower perceived quality, a perceptual gate softens the ranking targets of pairs with small perceptual differences in rendered views. The synthetic supervision is used only during training and needs no target-domain data. In a single training run on SJTU-PCQA, PGS-PCQA achieves Spearman rank correlation coefficients (SRCCs) of 0.709 on WPC and 0.751 on BASICS. The corresponding published DSP-PCQA scores are 0.595 and 0.723. Under reference-disjoint cross-validation, PGS-PCQA achieves SRCCs of 0.955 on SJTU-PCQA, 0.934 on WPC, 0.906 on BASICS, and 0.791 on LS-PCQA Part I. In the exclusion experiment, the reported scores for the reduced synthetic bank represent 58-65% of the full-bank SRCC gain relative to training without the bank. Code is available at https://github.com/Fan-QY/PGS-PCQA.

title: EAGLE: Entity-Aware Grounding with Layered Evidence for High-Resolution Image Understanding
abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) still struggle with fine-grained understanding of high-resolution images: attention heads vary in their reliability for grounding target entities and their attributes, while localized details are often disconnected from the broader scene context. We propose EAGLE (Entity-Aware Grounding with Layered Evidence for High-Resolution Image Understanding), a plug-in framework that jointly selects grounding signals and organizes hierarchical visual evidence. EAGLE employs a fine-grained dataset to screen visually-grounded attention heads, followed by entity-aware grounding to extract target-specific regions. It then integrates hierarchical evidence construction and question-guided routing to select optimal view combinations, feeding them into the frozen MLLM to enhance fine-grained visual understanding. Experiments with Qwen2.5-VL-7B and InternVL3-8B demonstrate that EAGLE consistently improves performance across both backbones and achieves SOTA results on V*, HRBench-4K, and HRBench-8K compared with existing methods using the same backbone.

title: Seabird-Aware Multi-Objective Offshore Wind Capacity Allocation: A Gippsland Case Study
abstract: Offshore wind planning requires balancing capital cost, wind-resource potential, and seabird exposure. We formulate a spatial tri-objective mixed-integer linear program for offshore wind capacity allocation, minimizing capital cost and modeled seabird exposure while maximizing wind-weighted capacity. Applied to Australia's Gippsland offshore wind area, the model identifies exposure reductions of 23-44% at capital-cost premiums of 0.8-6.1% across 15 wind-weighted capacity requirements. We benchmark exposure-aware optimization against 19 percentile-based exclusion thresholds. At a fixed wind-weighted capacity requirement, the 5th-percentile threshold reduces exposure by 30.1% at a 37.6% cost premium, versus at least 30.1% at a 1.4% premium with optimization. Under a fixed capital budget, exclusion screening reduces exposure by 48.2% with a 26.9% capacity loss, compared with 48.5% and 7.6%, respectively, under optimization. These results highlight the value of explicitly optimizing graded seabird exposure.

title: AetherMemory: Memory Lifecycle Integrity in Autonomous Multi-Agent Systems
abstract: AetherMemory is the twelfth candidate of the Aether family. It investigates whether persistent knowledge in autonomous multi-agent systems requires a distinct architectural dimension — a memory lifecycle — that cannot be reduced to storage (AetherGit), consistency (AetherMesh), policy (AetherPolicy), or audit (AetherAudit). Current status: Phase 0 (Architectural Hypothesis). Decision: (E) Undetermined (interim). No implementation exists. There is no src/, no tests/, no experiments/. The investigation is analytical. The repository contains: - The architectural hypothesis, with seven lifecycle stages (S1–S7) and five candidate responsibilities (M1–M5). - A responsibility boundary map against the eleven other Aether projects. - A falsification plan with four failure conditions (M-F1 to M-F4). - Partial execution of M-F1 (coverage analysis), M-F2 (composition analysis), and M-F3 (decentralization analysis). - A status declaration for M-F4 (not executable at Phase 0, requires Phase 5 and 6). - An independence decision: (E) Undetermined (interim). - An independent review by Jonathan Rabe (AI | ML Engineer, Angeles University Foundation), completed 2026-11-19. The reviewer confirmed the (E) Undetermined (interim) classification. - A research paper (v0.1.0), 9 figures, and full project documentation. Structural dependency: AetherMemory is structurally dependent on the resolution of AetherPolicy and AetherAudit, both paused at Phase 4. Any conclusion about AetherMemory is conditional on how those two investigations resolve. AetherMemory is a candidate, not a result.

title: Coupling-Aware Reinforcement Learning for Co-Evolving Graph Games
abstract: Building hydrogen station networks, electric vehicle charging grids, or vaccine distribution systems requires coordinating two separately operated graphs, demand-side facilities and the supply-side networks they depend on, where each operator's payoff depends on the other's choices. We formalize this as the Co-Evolving Graph Game (CEGG), a setting that sits between facility location, interdependent-network analysis, and graph-based multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) but is not jointly addressed by any of them. We propose Cross-Graph Attention with Policy Mirror Descent (CGA-PMD), pairing cross-graph attention, which lets each agent read only the partner-graph nodes structurally coupled to its own, with a policy mirror descent update for stable training. Across three reward domains and a range of practical network scales, we find that the structure of the coupling selects which method wins: at small scale most methods are competitive, but as scale grows or coupling becomes irregular, CGA-PMD is the one method that stays reliable: it attains the highest success count on each of five real city networks, while own-only, unmasked-attention, and Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO)-based variants degrade in distinct ways. Our theoretical analysis addresses the optimizer side: the Kullback-Leibler (KL)-regularized update admits an iteration-uniform cumulative drift bound, whereas the clip update admits no such bound on the iterations where the clip does not bind. The implementation is available at https://github.com/Mina-Kim-Github/cegg-cga-pmd.

evidence.title: Coupling-Aware Reinforcement Learning for Co-Evolving Graph Games
evidence.abstract: Building hydrogen station networks, electric vehicle charging grids, or vaccine distribution systems requires coordinating two separately operated graphs, demand-side facilities and the supply-side networks they depend on, where each operator's payoff depends on the other's choices. We formalize this as the Co-Evolving Graph Game (CEGG), a setting that sits between facility location, interdependent-network analysis, and graph-based multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) but is not jointly addressed by any of them. We propose Cross-Graph Attention with Policy Mirror Descent (CGA-PMD), pairing cross-graph attention, which lets each agent read only the partner-graph nodes structurally coupled to its own, with a policy mirror descent update for stable training. Across three reward domains and a range of practical network scales, we find that the structure of the coupling selects which method wins: at small scale most methods are competitive, but as scale grows or coupling becomes irregular, CGA-PMD is the one method that stays reliable: it attains the highest success count on each of five real city networks, while own-only, unmasked-attention, and Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO)-based variants degrade in distinct ways. Our theoretical analysis addresses the optimizer side: the Kullback-Leibler (KL)-regularized update admits an iteration-uniform cumulative drift bound, whereas the clip update admits no such bound on the iterations where the clip does not bind. The implementation is available at https://github.com/Mina-Kim-Github/cegg-cga-pmd.

title: Redesigning Neural Networks to Not be Confidently Wrong even to Strong Adversarial Attacks
abstract: Early deep learning models attempted to simulate visual perception using a neural hierarchy that alternated between two types of layer: one modelled on cortical simple cells (that was designed to increase selectivity), and one modelled on cortical complex cells (that aimed to increase tolerance). We show that such a neural network (NN) architecture, when implemented with novel components that are better able to learn selective and tolerant representations, is capable of accurate and robust image classification and improved alignment between the behaviour of the model and the perceptual abilities of humans. Firstly, the proposed models are shallow, fewer than ten layer-pairs, which is more consistent with the rapid feedforward object categorisation performed by the biological visual system. Secondly, they are far less prone to producing classification predictions with high confidence for samples from unknown classes or for image consisting of pure noise, and hence, like humans are not easily fooled into perceiving objects that are not present in the image. Thirdly, for the proposed NNs adversarial samples cause predictions with low confidence, enabling them to be accurately identified. In contrast to humans, our networks still do not correctly classify adversarial samples. However, the behaviour of our networks is a significant step towards human-like behaviour compared to standard DNNs that produce highly confident, but incorrect, classification predictions for adversarial samples. The increased robustness to adversarial and unknown samples is achieved while maintaining competitive performance in terms of generalisation to novel samples from the training categories. This enables models of this type to be competitive with state-of-the-art DNNs across multiple different evaluation metrics and benchmark tasks.

title: Breaking the Barrier of Hard Samples: A Data-Centric Approach to Synthetic Data for Medical Tasks
abstract: Data scarcity and quality issues remain significant barriers to developing robust predictive models in medical research. Traditional reliance on real-world data often leads to biased models with poor generalizability across diverse patient populations. Synthetic data generation has emerged as a promising solution, yet challenges related to these samples' representativeness and effective utilization persist. This paper introduces Profile2Gen, a novel data-centric framework designed to guide the generation and refinement of synthetic data, focusing on addressing hard-to-learn samples in regression tasks. We conducted approximately 18,000 experiments to validate its effectiveness across six medical datasets, utilizing seven state-of-the-art generative models. Results demonstrate that refined synthetic samples can reduce predictive errors and enhance model reliability. Additionally, we generalize the DataIQ framework to support regression tasks, enabling its application in broader contexts. Statistical analyses confirm that our approach achieves equal or superior performance compared to models trained exclusively on real data.

title: Semiparametric Efficiency for Entropic Optimal Transport under Structured Distribution Shift
abstract: Can structural information improve estimation of entropic optimal transport (EOT), and when is the gain zero? We study a fixed-dimensional exponential density ratio model (DRM) with a nonparametric baseline, compact support, and fixed positive regularization. At positive limiting sampling fractions, an exact projection identity quantifies the variance gain from the restriction. The pooled empirical-likelihood estimator attains the restricted bound and supports asymptotically valid confidence intervals when the bound is positive. Even under correct specification, the gain can be zero and can shrink as the tilt space expands. The same projection residual determines direction-specific first-order bias under local misspecification. When both samples grow and the target fraction vanishes, a zero first-order tilt derivative can leave source fluctuations and quadratic tilt error as the leading terms. Their balance gives a phase transition in the limiting distribution. A continuous example gives different convergence rates for two correctly specified bases at the same distribution pair. Controlled experiments assess the fixed-proportion theory. Natural-data comparisons distinguish variance reductions from improvements in reference RMSE driven by smaller reference bias.

title: $R^2$: Recognizing and Reducing Redundant Visual Tool Use
abstract: Recent studies have shown that visual tools can improve multimodal reasoning. However, the effects of tools vary substantially across samples, and benchmark accuracy alone does not reveal whether tool interactions are beneficial or redundant. We present $R^2$, a framework that recognizes and reduces redundant visual tool use in vision-language models. We first introduce a sample-level Category Analysis of Tool Utility (CAT), which categorizes samples according to whether a model can benefit from tools. This analysis reveals that benchmark scores may obscure a model's tool-use ability. Across seven benchmarks, samples benefiting from tools account for at most 12.44% of each benchmark, while the majority gain little from tool interaction or are even harmed by it. To assess individual calls, we propose the Visual Feedback Dependency (VFD) metric, which compares the likelihood of the same subsequent reasoning under actual and alternative visual feedback without an external evaluator or trajectory regeneration. Redundancy-Aware GRPO (RA-GRPO) combines this dependency signal with a category-conditioned base call cost to assign relative efficiency advantages among correct trajectories, supplementing outcome-based supervision. Across the seven benchmarks, RA-GRPO reduces the mean number of tool calls by 12.39% relative to Vanilla GRPO at comparable benchmark accuracy. Evaluated by tool-utility category, RA-GRPO improves category macro-average accuracy over Vanilla GRPO by 3.35 percentage points.

title: Two Actions from One State: Fork Futures Teach JEPA World Models to Compare
abstract: JEPA world models are trained to predict logged transitions but used to compare counterfactual actions from one state. The logged behavior data show one action per state, and under a local linear approximation we prove the action response is unidentified along any direction the policy never varies within a state. We therefore supplement behavior data with measured outcomes of alternative actions from the same state. Our fork futures execute two actions from one restored state, and their outcome difference cancels the state term, identifying the action response on the sampled span. The resulting model, Fork-JEPA, matches predicted to measured differences, anchors the logged successor with behavior prediction, and adds a lookback head that keeps the predecessor recoverable, all at training time, leaving planning unchanged. On three visual control tasks, behavior-only training leaves the predicted action effect no better than a constant guess. Fork-JEPA makes it readable and raises planning success by up to 14\% over LeWM, its base model. Where the action response changes across hidden zones, it nearly doubles cross-zone success, and 1,024 fork pairs beat 1.2M extra behavior steps. Our project is available at https://fork-jepa.github.io/.

title: SAMA: Training-Free Consensus Ridge Tracking for Camera-Based Heart Rate on Five Public Datasets
abstract: Remote photoplethysmography (rPPG) is usually benchmarked by one heart rate per video, a figure that hides the short windows in which a tele-consultation would actually read the pulse. We present SAMA, a training-free estimator that (i) forms a quality-weighted consensus of POS and CHROM chrominance spectra, (ii) discounts frequencies occupied by pulse-free references derived from the same frames (frame motion, skin-mask geometry and background brightness), (iii) follows the heart rate through time with a Viterbi ridge under a random-walk prior, and (iv) returns a track-filtered, amplitude-normalised waveform with a per-window confidence. No parameter is learned and no dataset-specific tuning is used. On 218 recordings from 111 participants in five public datasets (UBFC-rPPG, PURE, SUMS, M3PD and a two-participant subset of MMPD), all processed with the same fixed face box and scored with a re-implementation of the rPPG-Toolbox protocol, SAMA has the lowest mean absolute error (MAE) averaged over datasets at every protocol level: 4.40 against 5.13,bpm for POS per video, 4.80 against 5.43 on 30,s windows and 5.05 against 6.59 on 10,s windows. Pooled over participants, the bootstrap interval of its paired difference from POS excludes zero on 30,s and 10,s windows (Wilcoxon p=0.11 and 0.004) but not per video, and it does not beat POS on SUMS per video or on the MMPD subset. Withholding the 20\% least confident windows lowers the pooled 10,s error from 4.06 to 2.33,bpm. We also show that the per-video protocol has a floor of 1.2--1.6,bpm on datasets where heart rate drifts, and that skin tone cannot be recovered from uncalibrated video, which motivates the instrumented, skin-tone-stratified collection we propose for the Indian population. The method does not surpass the best published neural networks on UBFC-rPPG; we report where it stands against them without re-running them.

title: SLP-Bench: Evaluating and Improving Acoustic Claims of Reasoning Audio Language Models on Clinical Speech
abstract: Audio language models (ALMs) can answer clinical questions from speech, outperforming baselines built on handcrafted acoustic features. Reasoning ALMs generate a chain of thought that refers to properties of the speaker's voice before predicting. Each statement the model makes about the voice needs to be checked against clinicians' perceptual ratings of the same recording. On clinical speech, existing evaluations score only the final answer. We introduce Speech Language Pathologist Bench (SLP-Bench), a benchmark grading each acoustic claim in the chain of thought against clinicians' perceptual ratings of the same recording. It covers five clinician-rated datasets and 25 perceptual dimensions, and assesses claims for factuality, stability under resampling, and consistency across reworded and different questions. Across ten open-weight reasoning ALMs evaluated zero-shot, claim balanced accuracy ranges from 0.52 to 0.58, claims change under resampling and rewording, and the most consistent models are not the most factual. Fine-tuning a 7B ALM with GRPO on a reward for claims that agree with clinicians raises its claim balanced accuracy from 0.54 to 0.60 and its mean kappa from 0.39 to 0.61, while preserving answer accuracy on per-dimension questions. SLP-Bench is available upon request, subject to approval by the providers of each dataset.

title: No Perfect Guardrail & No Perfect Guard: On the Decidability of Output Policies for Large Language Models
abstract: Expecting guardrails to provide a general guarantee of safety fails to recognize the limits of computational enforcement and policy specification. We argue that promising such perfection is an ethical failure of precision, and that invoking it to abdicate responsibility is a moral failure. Guardrails can support responsible action, but cannot relieve researchers, developers, policymakers, or users of their obligations to examine what they claim, permit, and prevent. We establish a precise computational boundary. If every finite string is a possible output of a language model, a computable guard that blocks every forbidden output and passes every permitted one exists if and only if the policy is decidable. For an undecidable policy, every guard misclassifies infinitely many strings, and every guard that blocks all forbidden outputs excludes infinitely many permitted ones. We apply this characterization to arithmetic truth, program behavior, and harmful instructions to an idealized recipient. We distinguish guards from execution monitors, identify bounded and interceptable cases admitting exact enforcement, and explain why the results establish no positive lower bound on average error. Exact enforcement does not establish that a policy adequately captures safety. Conservative exclusion may withhold warnings, remedies, or challenges needed to recognize the policy's own defects. Human oversight cannot substitute for judgment: an apparent controller can become an instrument of purposes they have ceased to examine. Responsible governance requires continued critical challenge and the intellectual and moral humility to recognize possible flaws in our machines, rules, policies, and ourselves. The impossibility of a general assurance of perfection is a condition responsible practice must confront, not a responsibility that another guardrail - or another guard - can remove.

title: Decision Models Are General-Purpose Process Reward Models
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) from verifiable outcomes gives a language agent one reward per episode: every step is credited alike, and nothing about the task is learned when all rollouts fail. The last mile, step-level credit, usually requires step labels, a learned critic, costly LLM judges or hand-written rules. We introduce DM-PRM, which turns a general-purpose decision model -- one answering yes/no questions with probabilities -- into a general-purpose process reward model (PRM), zero-shot: no step labels, no fine-tuning, no critic. DM-PRM asks one question per step and adds the standardised answers to the advantage. It plugs into any policy-gradient method; one model, with one question text per environment, serves household tasks, web shopping and multiple RL methods. With Qwen2.5-1.5B it lifts GRPO by over twenty points on ALFWorld and over ten on WebShop, overtakes GiGPO on ALFWorld and learns in far fewer iterations; it also improves GiGPO and GraphGPO on both benchmarks and reaches the highest success of our comparison, ahead of critic-based PPO and of state-of-the-art GiGPO, HGPO and GraphGPO. Its scores locate useful steps in failed rollouts, and trained agents drop idle actions and explore instead of circling. DM-PRM shows that step credit need not be learned: it can be asked for.

title: A Continual Self-Supervised Learning Framework Using a Decoder and a Clustering-Based Data Selection Method
abstract: Continual learning aims to learn a sequence of tasks without forgetting the previously learned tasks. Promising methods for achieving continual learning include applying a replay buffer that stores previously learned samples in existing learning frameworks. Among these methods, lifelong unsupervised mixup (LUMP) interpolates the current task samples and samples from the replay buffer to prevent forgetting. LUMP randomly selects data for the replay buffer. This random selection is likely to have a negative effect on learning performance. In this study, we propose a clustering-based data selection method for the replay buffer. In addition, we introduce a denoising autoencoder to the self-supervised methods to improve the performance of the learning representations. We compare the clustering algorithms used in our framework and demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework through computational experiments. Experimental results on CIFAR-100 and Tiny-ImageNet demonstrate that the proposed framework improves the average accuracy compared with LUMP while reducing forgetting. In particular, the CA+-based selection approach enhances the learning performance. The source code is available at https://github.com/Masuyama-lab/LUMP_SidAE_Clustering

title: Grammar-as-a-Drafter: More Tokens per Speculative Decoding Step on Grammar-Constrained Structured Outputs
abstract: Speculative decoding speeds up generation by letting a lightweight drafter propose tokens that the target model verifies in one forward pass. Under structured outputs (JSON schemas, regular expressions, tool-call formats), the drafter works against a constraint it does not know, so its proposals for keys, delimiters, and indentation are often rejected or invalid, even though the grammar engine already knows the next tokens. We present Grammar-as-a-Drafter (GaaD), which makes the grammar a second drafter. Before each verify step, the scheduler merges the drafter's proposal with grammar-forced tokens (out-degree 1 in the grammar automaton) into one draft row of width $K$ (which can exceed the drafter's proposal length $K_M$): matching tokens are promoted to GRAMMAR, the proposal is truncated where it disagrees, and grammar tokens fill the remaining slots. The verify step accepts GRAMMAR drafts without computing their logits, composing with any drafter without adding kernels or compilation on the critical path. Because grammars fix text rather than tokens, accepting canonical GRAMMAR drafts with probability 1 preserves grammar validity but can shift the output distribution relative to grammar-masked decoding. We implement GaaD in vllm-torchtpu and an independent Rust serving runtime, and evaluate it on TPU v7x with MTP, DFlash, and n-gram drafters on a JSON character-profile benchmark. GaaD raises average acceptance length from 2.06 to 5.43 for MTP (Qwen3.5-0.8B; 1.99 to 5.31 on Qwen3.5-35B-A3B), 1.57 to 4.13 for DFlash, and 1.30 to 3.64 for n-gram (Qwen3-4B), decoding 2.66-2.81x faster at batch size 1 and 1.14-1.70x faster at batch size 64. In the Rust runtime, MTP with GaaD is 2.23x faster on Qwen3.5-0.8B and 2.02x on Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-FP8 (1.22-1.69x at high concurrency). Under mixed traffic, GaaD finishes workloads 1.03-1.23x sooner while modestly raising plain-text TPOT.

GaaD raises average acceptance length from 2.06 to 5.43 for MTP (Qwen3.5-0.8B; 1.99 to 5.31 on Qwen3.5-35B-A3B), 1.57 to 4.13 for DFlash, and 1.30 to 3.64 for n-gram (Qwen3-4B), decoding 2.66-2.81x faster at batch size 1 and 1.14-1.70x faster at batch size 64. In the Rust runtime, MTP with GaaD is 2.23x faster on Qwen3.5-0.8B and 2.02x on Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-FP8 (1.22-1.69x at high concurrency). Under mixed traffic, GaaD finishes workloads 1.03-1.23x sooner while modestly raising plain-text TPOT.

title: DOiT: Better Money-Flow Ranking Can Coexist with Worse Account Selection in Anti-Money Laundering Review
abstract: Anti-money laundering (AML) review selects suspicious accounts and reconstructs transfers. Downstream graph neural networks (GNNs) rank money-flow evidence but may also reorder the account queue. DOiT separates these decisions at equal review capacity: account selection determines where graph investigation starts. Across AMLWorld and AMLNet, GNN reordering harms higher-yield upstream orders but helps lower-yield ones. On AMLWorld, this harm coexists with higher transaction average precision (AP) in dimension-matched, per-run decoders, demonstrating separable ranking abilities. At small capacities, positive neighbors can displace a denser upstream prefix and lower yield; replacement costs fall as that prefix is exhausted, allowing the preferred order to reverse. A restricted-access synthetic benchmark informed by real transaction patterns reproduces this separation and validation-based upstream preservation. Capacity-matched combination protects upstream ordering while retaining GNN money-flow analysis, admitting GNN queue influence only where held-out evidence supports it.

title: Self-Supervised Continuous-Time Depth Learning and Ego-Motion Estimation from Asynchronous Events
abstract: Event cameras register brightness changes pixel by pixel with microsecond precision, whereas the dense depth that could supervise them is costly to acquire and exists only at isolated instants. Condensing the stream into frames eases learning, but at the expense of the very timing that sets event sensing apart. We propose a self-supervised approach in which each event is assigned its own depth in continuous time, and the camera motion is recovered from the same observations. Supervision arises from geometry: lifted into 3D by its predicted depth and displaced by the camera motion at the instant it fired, an event should coincide with others produced by the same edge, so any misalignment exposes an error in depth or motion. Differentiable rendering then turns these per-event estimates into dense depth maps at target times within each window, faithful to the events behind them. On MVSEC, the approach outperforms prior event-only self-supervised methods in most sequences and depth ranges, with the widest margins at night, and recovers camera rotation more accurately than an earlier unsupervised event-based method. Ablations isolate the roles of local spatiotemporal context, the temporal backbone, and the alignment objective. These results position motion-compensated event alignment as a principled source of supervision for continuous-time depth and ego-motion estimation.

title: A preference for local interaction between layers emerges during training
abstract: A deep neural network is a stack of layers, and all layers are trained to lower one shared error. A change in one layer can therefore reach every other layer. Because the error is shared by all layers, one would expect the other layers to respond alike, whether they are next to the changed layer or far from it. We find that early in training the response is weak and its order by distance is not stable. As training proceeds, the response grows, and neighboring layers come to respond to changes in each other more strongly than layers further apart, in almost every network. This locality forms during training, although training links every layer to every other. We show this by pushing one layer of a copy of the network at many stages of training and measuring how much of the push reaches each of the other layers. The experiments use 512 five-layer networks trained on modular addition with each of two optimizers, AdamW and stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics.

title: Online Learning for Minimizing Maximum Tardiness in Single-Machine Scheduling
abstract: We study online learning for minimizing maximum tardiness (\OMMT) in single-machine scheduling. In each round, the learner selects a permutation of \(n\) fixed jobs, representing a schedule. The environment then reveals a processing time and a due date for each job, and the learner incurs a vector-valued loss whose components correspond to the tardiness of the individual jobs. The goal of the learner is to minimize \(α\)-regret, the difference between the learner's maximum cumulative tardiness and \(α\) times that of the best fixed permutation in hindsight, for as small \(α\) as possible. We investigate OMMT under both stochastic and adversarial environments. In the stochastic setting, we prove that the expected \(1\)-regret of the Follow-the-Leader (FTL) algorithm is \( O\!\left(\frac{n\log n}{Δ^2}\right) \), together with a corresponding high-probability bound, where \(Δ\) is a distribution-dependent gap parameter. At round \(t \in \{1,\dots,T\}\), FTL runs in \(O(tn^2)\) time and \(O(tn)\) space. In the adversarial setting, we prove that, for any \(0<c<\log_2 n/16\), the \(α\)-regret is \(Ω(T)\) whenever \(α<\log_2 n/16-c\). We then reduce OMMT to a surrogate online learning problem and apply Follow-the-Perturbed-Leader (FTPL), obtaining an expected \(α\)-regret bound of \(O(n^2\sqrt{T})\) for \(α=O(\log n)\). Thus, the logarithmic dependence of \(α\) on \(n\) is tight up to constant factors. Each FTPL update admits a mixed-integer programming formulation whose size is polynomial in \(n\) and \(t\).

title: Every Man Must Play a Part: After Hinton's Alarm
abstract: In two years the range of tasks AI systems can carry out has grown sharply, and they can now plan a task, execute it and evaluate the result in a cycle. The autonomous operation of machines has advanced in parallel, and AI now reaches physical space. What remains is adjustment and resources, and areas that do not yet pay are already objects of investment, because costs are certain to fall. The reach of AI ethics widens with this, from the behaviour of a system to the society it acts in. That something large is under way is widely sensed, and in November 2026 Geoffrey Hinton, a pioneer of the field, carried that sense as a warning to European Union leaders. The path from the widening to the conclusions drawn has not been set out. This commentary asks what follows from the widening and what does not. It examines the alarm's reasoning, which derives loss of control from a ranking of intelligence, a machine that wants and a competition that one party loses. It then turns from AI's position on a line of capability to how systems and their society are built: what it takes to understand an instruction, who answers for each component, and how harm arises where no machine wants anything and no builder intends it. The starting point is that a system as large as a society cannot be inferred from individual pieces of logic. On that view humankind is one system, with AI part of it.

title: SMAD: A Semantics-Guided Multi-Agent Framework for Unsupervised Time-Series Anomaly Detection
abstract: Time-series anomaly detection (TSAD) lacks a one-size-fits-all detector for heterogeneous data and anomaly types. Existing automation is limited by implicit objectives, potentially unreliable historical knowledge, or high computational costs. More fundamentally, it selects how to detect anomalies without explicitly defining what to detect. We propose SMAD, an LLM-based multi-agent framework that translates anomaly intent into executable, testable detection pipelines. Rather than selecting detectors against an implicit target, SMAD establishes a natural-language semantic contract grounded in measurable time-series properties, specifying target event patterns, expected score responses, and validation questions. This contract governs both detector construction and evaluation: LLM agents propose pipelines, while contract-matched synthetic interventions provide label-free evidence from the target series to assess semantic coverage and guide iterative self-refinement. A semantics-aware ensemble integrates validated candidates and attributes each alert to contributing detectors and supporting evidence. On univariate and multivariate TSAD benchmarks, SMAD improves detection performance over the strongest baseline by 11.5% and 9.6%, respectively, while outperforming general-purpose coding agents at 2-5x lower language-model token cost.

title: $\mathtt{DistP}$: Scaling Local-Update Training with Zero-Shot Hyperparameter Transfer
abstract: Local-update methods offer a communication-efficient alternative to Distributed Data Parallelism ($\mathtt{DDP}$), but introduce additional hyperparameters that require costly tuning. For $\mathtt{DDP}$, zero-shot hyperparameter transfer reduces this cost by reusing settings tuned on smaller models, but its applicability to local-update training remains unclear. We propose $\mathtt{DistP}$, a theoretical framework extending existing transfer rules from $\mathtt{DDP}$ to local-update training with varying worker counts, local steps, and outer optimizers. With averaging as the outer optimizer, $\mathtt{DistP}$ supports learning-rate transfer across width and depth while improving model quality. The tuned inner learning rate also directly transfers across synchronization intervals, but follows two regimes when increasing the global batch size: square-root learning-rate scaling for larger local batches and a fixed reference rate for additional workers. We then generalize width and depth transfer to other outer optimizers, enabling stable scaling with $\mathtt{Adam}$. However, with momentum in the outer optimizer, changing batch size or local steps can require inner--outer learning-rate tuning, consistent with prior work. In language-modeling experiments at $823$M parameters, $\mathtt{DistP}$ reduces validation loss by $8.1\%$ and improves mean downstream accuracy by $10\%$ relative to baselines without retuning at the larger scale. Fitted scaling laws suggest that this advantage grows with the compute budget, reinforcing the benefits of $\mathtt{DistP}$ for communication-efficient training.

title: How Many Bytes Has a BPE Model Seen? Estimating Byte-Token Exposure in Pretraining from Corpus Statistics and Embedding Norms
abstract: Byte-level BPE vocabularies retain 256 single-byte fallback tokens. When converting such a model into a pure byte-level model, these tokens provide the starting embeddings. How much training have they received? We estimate byte-token exposure in Qwen3.8 using two independent routes. First, we tokenize 540 MB of public corpora covering 40 domains and 33 languages, then combine per-domain token shares with assumed pretraining mixtures. Single-byte tokens account for 13 to 36% of tokens, mostly ASCII; genuine UTF-8 fallback bytes (0x80-0xFF) account for 0.15 to 0.27% under mainstream mixtures, or about 2 billion occurrences per trillion pretraining tokens. Fallback rates vary by four orders of magnitude across languages, reflecting how well each script is covered by the vocabulary. Second, we analyze embedding and output-matrix row norms for four open models, using untrained padding rows as a zero-exposure baseline and ordinary tokens with known frequencies for calibration. In all four models, the 13 bytes that cannot occur in valid UTF-8 remain at initialization, while every legal high byte lies in a high-frequency band. For Qwen3.8, the norm-based estimate agrees with the corpus estimate within a factor of four. The norm-frequency relation eventually folds, so inversion is useful only as a model-specific, order-of-magnitude estimate. No private data were used.

title: Proactive Defense Benchmark against Deepfake Generation
abstract: Despite the proliferation of proactive defenses against deepfakes, the lack of a unified evaluation protocol precludes fair comparison and masks critical vulnerabilities. To bridge this gap, we present the first comprehensive benchmark that systematically assesses disruption, robustness, and transferability encompassing pixel, perceptual, and identity metrics. Our extensive analysis reveals that fidelity and identity metrics capture orthogonal performance axes, often leading to conflicting interpretations when relied upon individually. Furthermore, we identify a fundamental trade-off where peak white-box performance signals overfitting, and we introduce a calibrated evaluation to correct generator-induced identity bias. By exposing these blind spots, we establish a rigorous standard to guide the development of genuinely generalizable protections. Project page is available at: https://proactivedefensebenchmark.github.io/
