title: COMPASS: Cross-modal Observation with Multi-Path Adaptive Stopping and Selection for Early Time Series Classification
abstract: Early time-series classification (ETSC) balances predictive performance against the amount of observed data. In multimodal settings, modality-associated and fused branches may differ in predictive ability at the same observed prefix, motivating joint decisions about when to stop and which branch should provide the final prediction. We propose COMPASS, a two-stage framework that preserves two modality-associated temporal branches and one fusion branch. The first stage combines cross-modal feature exchange and gated fusion with branch-wise supervision at every prefix. The second stage optimizes a shared four-action controller to continue observation or terminate through one of the frozen branches. Experiments on six physiological and wearable datasets compare COMPASS with multimodal adaptations of five ETSC baselines. COMPASS achieves the best average ranks in accuracy-earliness harmonic mean, AUROC, and earliness within this comparison set. At identical learned stopping times, branch selection improves mean accuracy over fusion readout on five of the six datasets, with gains of 2.35 and 2.16 percentage points on ISRUC-Sleep and UCDDB, respectively. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work on joint stopping and branch selection for multimodal early time series classification.

title: Vertical Domain Large Language Models: Applications, Challenges, Future Prospects
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have become a cornerstone of modern generative artificial intelligence, demonstrating remarkable performance across a wide range of tasks, including machine translation, question answering, and dialogue generation. However, most existing reviews primarily emphasize theoretical foundations and training methodologies, and offer limited insights into real-world application performance and domain-specific deployment patterns. To address this gap, we conducted a systematic literature review following PRISMA guidelines, synthesizing the application of LLMs across diverse vertical domains. The review examines system architectures, technical approaches, and performance benchmarks reported in the literature. In addition, it analyzes core challenges associated with LLM deployment, such as hallucinations, explainability, value alignment, and data quality, along with targeted solutions. Finally, it identifies emerging research opportunities and future directions, contributing to a more coherent, application-oriented understanding of LLM development and impact.

title: Defending Vision-Language-Action Models against Transferable Attacks via Visual-Proprioceptive Consistency
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have demonstrated strong capabilities in a wide range of robotic tasks. However, adversarial attacks in VLA models have shown strong transferability across robotic tasks, posing significant threats to robotic systems. Despite their different attack strategies, we observe that these transferable attacks share a common consequence: they disrupt the VLA model's perception towards the robot itself. Motivated by this observation, we propose a proprioception-grounded defense framework that leverages trusted proprioceptive information to detect and mitigate transferable adversarial attacks. Specifically, we utilize the robot's proprioceptive states to establish a trusted spatial reference, and compare it with the robot's perceived location inferred from visual features. Discrepancies between these two sources provide a reliable signal for detecting adversarial attacks. Extensive experiments demonstrate effective detection of transferable adversarial patches and improved closed-loop performance. Real-robot experiments further demonstrate the effectiveness of our defense on real-world robotic tasks.

title: Evaluating Prompting Strategies for Zero-Shot Multilingual Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis with Large Language Models
abstract: While large language models (LLMs) have advanced natural language understanding, their ability to perform complex target-aspect-sentiment detection (TASD) -- a key task within aspect-based sentiment analysis (ABSA) -- in zero-shot multilingual settings remains underexplored. Existing ABSA research predominantly focuses on English or relies on fine-tuned task-specific models, leaving a gap in understanding how open-weight LLMs handle compound sentiment triplet extraction across diverse language families and domains. We present a systematic evaluation of zero-shot multilingual TASD across 12 languages and three domains using seven instruction-tuned open-weight models -- ranging from 8B to 35B parameters across dense and mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures -- under four prompting paradigms: monolithic, chain-of-thought, sequential, and sequential refine. Our results show that direct monolithic prompting achieves strong zero-shot performance, outperforming multi-step pipelines, while dense models consistently outperform sparse MoE architectures. Through fine-grained error taxonomy profiling and step-level pipeline tracking, we demonstrate that initial aspect term recall forms a hard bottleneck, whereas multi-step decomposition degrades extraction quality; iterative refinement only partially recovers this loss on larger models while inducing net-negative over-refinement on smaller architectures. Finally, generation volume analysis shows that multi-step strategies incur up to 2.38x token overhead without F1 gains, establishing monolithic prompting as the most effective and efficient paradigm for multilingual ABSA.

title: The Assistant Persona Differs Across Languages in Activation Space
abstract: Large language models behave differently across languages, and are noticeably less safe in lower-resource languages. This gap is well established behaviorally, but not mechanistically. Directions in activation space, including the assistant persona direction, are almost always extracted from English and assumed to generalize across languages. We extract the assistant persona direction in 31 languages in Qwen3-32B, and find that the resulting axes differ substantially: their cosine similarity to the English axis ranges from 0.378 to 0.911. Moreover, each language's assistant persona direction and its magnitude are correlated with the language's resource level. We also find that the model's default assistant state is farther from the helpful assistant pole in lower-resource languages. Finally, steering against a language's own axis amplifies persona-based jailbreak more than steering against the English axis. These results indicate that the model does not carry a single assistant representation across languages. More broadly, the assistant persona may need to be an explicit target of multilingual alignment.

title: Beyond Prompt Imitation: Capability-Aware Video Generation with Smaller Models
abstract: Inference-time methods that lift a small open video generator toward a proprietary one are compared through preference scores, which never say how much of the gap to a target video they close. We introduce the oracle control ladder, which hands a fixed student progressively richer information from a target clip and reads the closure of each fidelity metric at each rung as an empirical headroom reference for the methods that must synthesize that information. On 954 clips of the principal student, a dense caption reproduces little of the appearance and almost none of the motion of a target, a first frame closes half of the appearance gap and a tenth of the motion gap, a depth video closes three quarters of the motion gap and leaves color untouched, and the two together close 64 to 94% of every fidelity gap across four teachers, while a second student agrees on the rungs that it accepts. An item response model forecasts which rung closes which clip with held-out AUC of 0.76 to 0.95 on the fidelity criteria and serves as the prior of a budgeted selection policy. When controls are free, a fixed dense-control rung is hard to improve upon, and once controls are priced the policy lies above the fixed-rung frontier at matched cost and survives critics that ruin critic-driven search.

title: Dynamic Token Merging for Efficient Vision-Language Models
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) represent each image with hundreds of visual tokens, which can make inference costly even when a prompt depends on only part of the image. Dynamic Token Merging (DTM), introduced in MrT5 for byte-level text encoders, learns which tokens to remove: a lightweight delete gate scores contextualized hidden states, acts as a differentiable attention bias during training, and physically removes tokens at inference. We argue that DTM is a general token deletion framework rather than a byte-level technique, and extend it to the vision modality and to decoder-only models. Applying DTM to T5Gemma 2 and Gemma 3 yields V-MrT5Gemma2, which deletes visual tokens inside a bidirectional multimodal encoder, and V-MrGemma3, which compacts the prompt and its key-value caches during decoder-only prefill. Across ten benchmarks, DTM's advantage over attention-based and random deletion grows with the deletion rate and is largest on document, chart, and scene-text reading. At 80% visual token deletion (approximately 60% fewer FLOPs), DTM raises accuracy over FastV from 51.8 to 63.0 on ChartQA and from 63.3 to 67.8 on TextVQA with V-MrT5Gemma2, as well as from 62.2 to 68.8 and from 71.2 to 75.1 with V-MrGemma3, retaining 90-96% of unpruned performance on both tasks with significant efficiency gains. These results support DTM as a general framework for efficient transformers.

title: Toward Adversarially Robust World Models
abstract: Latent dynamic world models have proven to be highly versatile tools for embodied artificial intelligence systems, enabling online action planning, safe policy evaluation, and scalable policy learning. However, this versatility makes world models a vulnerable and centralized point of failure as a compromised model can impact planning, evaluation, and training at once. Therefore it is critical that the security and robustness properties of world models are properly understood before they are universally deployed in embodied AI systems. In this work we take a unifying approach towards this understanding, developing two novel attacks against world models, named state hallucination and dynamic shift attacks, aimed directly at impacting downstream systems, and proposing a new theoretical lens through which to study the robustness of latent dynamic world models. Through our analysis we identify robust latent space encoders as the key component of robust world models. We empirically validate this finding on four separate latent dynamic world model families, studying Dino World Model, Le World Model, r2Dreamer, and Cosmos 3, demonstrating significant improvements in robustness through adversarial encoder model training.

title: Beyond Outlier Rejection: Transient-Aware Reconstruction of Multi-Stack MRI
abstract: Clinical MRI typically acquires the organ of interest as consecutive stacks of 2D slices in different orientations. Reconstruction methods such as SVRTK and NeSVoR fuse them into one volume and down-weight what does not fit, although in living tissue the change during the scan is often the signal itself and can contain clinically relevant physiological information, such as fetal motion and uterine contraction. We propose an analysis-by-synthesis decomposition that explains every acquired voxel through its exact acquisition geometry as a static anatomy shared by all stacks, a rigid and smooth non-rigid motion per stack, and a sparse transient field per stack for changes during one acquisition only. A robust reweighting keeps such changes out of the anatomy. The model is fitted per subject without training data, with one configuration for all datasets. On a digital phantom with known ground truth, static changes are kept entirely in the anatomy, and the transient field of the stack that saw a transient recovers 68% of it at 12mm radius. From identical inputs, the anatomy predicts held-out stacks better than SVRTK and NeSVoR on uterine (NCC 0.897 against 0.874 and 0.863, 123 patients) and on prostate MRI from unseen sites and scanners (0.847 against 0.795 and 0.757, 85 patients), and on fetal brain MRI as well as SVRTK and better than NeSVoR (0.771 against 0.763 and 0.747, 83 fetuses). The transient fields flag corrupted fetal slices with an AUROC of 0.94 against expert raters. As the input of a frozen anomaly detector trained on healthy subjects only, the anatomy localizes radiologist-delineated uterine lesions better than the SVRTK and NeSVoR volumes (AUROC 0.76 against 0.71 and 0.71, 37 patients).

title: Refrain: Learning Multi-Shot Consistency from Inconsistent References for A$^2$O Video Generation
abstract: A comic-book character, a photorealistic cityscape, an oil-painted coffee cup -- such stylistically diverse references provide visual guidance across shots and frames, yet generating a coherent multi-shot video that unifies their visual styles while preserving subject identities and scene content remains challenging. Existing methods maintain cross-shot continuity through additional attention control or memory processing. However, they struggle to resolve disparate per-shot styles or handle reference-target duration mismatches within a single framework. We introduce Refrain, a unified model that learns cross-shot consistency through a self-supervised reconstruction task. Reference clips from the same original video are deliberately perturbed with distinct visual edits, and the model recovers the unedited source footage under a shared style prompt. The resulting pipeline yields DurMix-300K, which pairs independently edited references of varying durations with their original videos. Operating on the A$^2$O principle (Any Reference, Any Duration, One Timeline), Refrain maps image and video references onto a shared temporal canvas without auxiliary conditioning modules. For evaluation, experiments show that standard CLIP or DINO metrics frequently overlook stylistic clashes or misinterpret intended narrative cuts as inconsistency. We propose Shot-Debiased Consistency (SDC), which uses an extensive real-video bank to establish a baseline for style variation associated with content changes within shots. By discounting this baseline divergence, SDC evaluates cross-shot style shifts against real-world distributions, where smaller residual differences indicate higher stylistic continuity. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Refrain achieves state-of-the-art performance in cross-shot consistency, while excelling at shot timing, reference adherence, and text alignment.

title: More Bits Won't Fix It: Diagnosing and Treating an Ill-Conditioned Backward Pass (A Case Study on Gemma-4)
abstract: During LoRA fine-tuning of Gemma-4 (12B and 31B) on long prompts, whether they contain CT images, natural photos, or about 2,000 tokens of text, bf16 and fp32 gradients agree in the upper third of the language model (cosine similarity 0.96 or above) but are nearly orthogonal in the lower third. On image prompts, we trace the effect to an ill-conditioned backward path. The fp32 gradient is unchanged by element-wise relative noise of $10^{-6}$ on hidden states, confirming that fp32 is a valid reference. At $10^{-4}$, however, its cosine similarity with the noise-free gradient falls below 0.9 in 7 of 10 measurements, whereas bf16 forward states differ from fp32 states by about 1% per token. State swaps and backward-only interventions localize this sensitivity in Gemma-4-12B to the MLPs of layers 19-21 at image-token positions, where the gradient can be dominated by a single low-information patch. Detaching that path in the backward pass (while leaving the forward pass unchanged) keeps the gradient stable at $10^{-4}$ (cosine similarity 0.97 or above across all five measurements), lowers the median pre-clipping gradient norm from 8.5 to 0.63, and improves validation loss on a CT lesion-grounding task from 0.336 $\pm$ 0.019 to 0.296 $\pm$ 0.003 (four seeds; every modified run beats every baseline run). The gain disappears when the lower layers are frozen, and an fp32 run still exhibits gradient spikes (maximum norm 39,862) and fails to match this improvement. These training results cover one task and one model.

title: V2VFusion: Text-Controlled Video-to-Video Diffusion for Degradation-Aware Video Fusion
abstract: Video fusion integrates complementary information in multiple source video streams into a single sequence for complete scene perception. Existing methods perform frame-wise fusion and lack unified spatio-temporal modeling across sequences, damaging temporal coherence across sequences. When dealing with degradations, they also ignore temporal dynamics and overload a single network with diverse degradations, leading to limited and imbalanced degradation suppression. To address these issues, we propose V2VFusion, the first unified video-to-video fusion framework that directly generates temporally coherent, high-quality fused videos from degraded multi-source inputs. By reformulating video fusion as a video-to-video conditional generation problem in latent diffusion space, our approach holistically models spatio-temporal dependencies across entire sequences and intrinsically ensures sequence-level consistency. On this basis, a text-guided degradation-conditioned ControlNet bridges high-level textual degradation descriptions with low-level visual priors, enabling interpretable and controllable guidance for structure-preserving fusion beyond purely data-driven conditioning. To handle heterogeneous and compound degradations, a state-modulated degradation-aware hierarchical mixture-of-experts module decouples expert selection into diffusion-state-aware filtering and degradation-aware routing. It prevents unreliable routing and fosters expert specialization to mitigate representation conflicts among diverse degradations. Experiments on infrared-visible, multi-exposure, and multi-focus video fusion tasks and complex degradations validate that V2VFusion surpasses existing methods in fusion quality and temporal stability. The code is available at https://github.com/ChenDoubleJ/V2VFusion.

title: Which Loans, Not How Many: Exactly Level-Invariant, Anytime-Valid Monitoring of Deployed Risk Models
abstract: A refinancing wave can change the number of mortgage prepayments without changing the relationship between scores and prepayment. In a logistic model, conditioning on the monthly count removes the intercept from the likelihood of which loans prepay. Our fixed-start slope product tests a lower bound on the calibration slope. At threshold 20 its probability of ever crossing under the null is at most 5%. The restarted level sum tracks departures from intercept tolerance. A confidence sequence estimates a constant slope, and the restart-intersection rule detects changes in that slope. A continuous mixture avoids the off-grid width floor of a discrete prior. On Freddie Mac loans, fixed-slope resampling reproduces 78% of maintained-model monthly AUC variance in development and 70% in the holdout (95% intervals 57-100% and 48-100%). From fresh holdout starts, the restarted level sum crosses on both paths, and the fixed-start slope product stays below threshold on both. The restart-intersection rule signals a downward change for the frozen model in April 2018 and an upward change for the maintained model in a supplementary run in August 2019.

title: ChildAI-Gov: An Evidence-Linked AI System for Assessing EdTech Policies Against Children's Digital Rights
abstract: We present ChildAI-Gov, an explainable AI system for assessing whether education-technology (EdTech) policies respect children's digital rights. Generative AI is reaching children's education faster than its governance can keep pace, yet checking a tool against children's rights remains manual, expert-dependent, and slow. We propose the Child Rights Impact Score (CRIS), an evidence-linked measure across five dimensions: safety, privacy, transparency, autonomy, and non-discrimination. ChildAI-Gov reads an EdTech tool's privacy or AI policy and scores each dimension by combining a large-language-model judgement (gpt-4o-mini) with a deterministic rule check. A retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) component grounds every score in the governing provisions, retrieved from a curated knowledge base of children's rights frameworks (the EU AI Act, UNICEF guidance, and others), so each score is tied to the evidence behind it and an auditor can trace which provision it rests on. We also construct AIPolicy-EdTech, a dataset of 57 real EdTech policies. On it, the five dimensions cohered as a single measure (Cronbach's alpha = 0.79), and grounding made scoring stricter while preserving rankings; an ungrounded baseline was far more lenient, passing nearly half the policies where ChildAI-Gov passed none. It offers evidence-linked decision support on documented commitments, not observation of real-world behaviour or determinations of legal compliance.

title: Solar-Conditioned Flow Matching for Multitemporal Aerial Visible-to-Infrared Image Translation
abstract: Aerial visible-to-infrared (V2IR) image translation provides scalable thermal data across the full diurnal cycle. However, existing methods predominantly learn a static mapping within narrow acquisition windows. As the thermal state evolves throughout the day, a single visible image may correspond to multiple plausible IR appearances, making V2IR translation an inherently multitemporal task. This letter proposes solar-conditioned latent flow matching (Solar-Flow), which upgrades aerial V2IR translation from static mapping to multitemporal generation. First, we design three computable physical factors, namely the solar elevation, the thermal phase clock (TPC), and the flight altitude. The TPC counts the elapsed heating and cooling hours on a continuous 24-hour axis anchored at sunrise, so the thermal state stays well defined even at hours without training samples. Second, we inject the condition into every Transformer block of a pretrained flow matching generator through adaptive layer normalization. This design preserves translation fidelity and enables multitemporal generation. Finally, we construct a paired aerial V2IR dataset covering 14 hour groups. Solar-Flow achieves multitemporal generation on this dataset, where a single visible image is translated into plausible IR images at multiple times of day, even at hours that were never seen in training.

title: WINSO: A Large-Size Very-High-Resolution Remote Sensing Dataset for Wind Turbine Detection and Solar Panel Segmentation
abstract: Wind and solar energy are central to the global transition toward net-zero emissions and sustainable development. Accurate spatial inventories of wind and solar facilities are essential for future energy planning. Satellite remote sensing provides a practical and efficient means to acquire such geospatial data at scale. However, reliable facility mapping from large-size satellite images remains constrained by the scarcity of carefully annotated datasets and the lack of systematic evaluation protocols. To address these limitations, we introduce \textbf{WINSO}, a large-scale wind and solar benchmark based on very-high-resolution (VHR) satellite imagery with ground sampling distances (GSDs) of 0.5--0.7\,m. WINSO comprises 10,962 large-size images sampled from diverse geographic locations across the Asia-Pacific region, covering at least 71,600\,$\text{km}^2$ and totaling 286.36 gigapixels, with individual image dimensions reaching 44,032$\times$62,208 pixels. Through manual annotation and expert verification, a total of 166,473 instances are labeled using horizontal bounding boxes (HBBs) for wind turbines and polygon masks for solar panels. To build baselines for clean-energy facility mapping, we evaluate state-of-the-art detection and segmentation models, specialized ultra-high-resolution (UHR) architectures, and vision-language models across different inference strategies. Furthermore, cross-dataset evaluations on two external public datasets illustrate the strong generalization capability of the WINSO. WINSO establishes a standardized benchmark to advance automated clean-energy mapping, paving the way for wide-area monitoring of the clean-energy transition.

WINSO comprises 10,962 large-size images sampled from diverse geographic locations across the Asia-Pacific region, covering at least 71,600\,$\text{km}^2$ and totaling 286.36 gigapixels, with individual image dimensions reaching 44,032$\times$62,208 pixels. Through manual annotation and expert verification, a total of 166,473 instances are labeled using horizontal bounding boxes (HBBs) for wind turbines and polygon masks for solar panels. To build baselines for clean-energy facility mapping, we evaluate state-of-the-art detection and segmentation models, specialized ultra-high-resolution (UHR) architectures, and vision-language models across different inference strategies. Furthermore, cross-dataset evaluations on two external public datasets illustrate the strong generalization capability of the WINSO. WINSO establishes a standardized benchmark to advance automated clean-energy mapping, paving the way for wide-area monitoring of the clean-energy transition.

title: PACE: Policy Augmentation and Compensation With Explicit Disturbance Estimation for Robust Locomotion
abstract: Reinforcement learning has made quadrupedal locomotion remarkably robust. To handle unmodeled dynamics and external disturbances, domain randomization is usually employed to make a policy hedge against every condition it might meet. However, maintaining accurate tracking across varying dynamics and generalizing beyond the sampled range remain challenging. Here we show that explicitly estimating the disturbance and feeding the resulting estimation back into both the policy and the controller can relax this compromise. We introduce Policy Augmentation and Compensation with Explicit disturbance estimation (PACE). The framework lumps payload variations, center-of-mass (CoM) shifts, actuator degradation, and external forces into one joint-space disturbance. A nonlinear observer subsequently recovers this disturbance online without requiring joint acceleration measurements. The disturbance estimation provides feedforward torque compensation as the foundational control pathway and further augments the policy observation to enable disturbance-aware action generation. Considering the learning difficulty of fast-varying contact effects, we further provide an analytical contact estimation approach from joint and inertial measurements, without demanding force sensors. Across eleven simulated dynamics conditions, PACE reduces velocity-tracking error by 18.1% to 57.0% against state-of-the-art baselines, and maintains improved tracking under out-of-distribution (OOD) commands. Notably, in real-world experiments, the deployed real robot carried an 11.5 kg payload, nearly equal to its own mass. It also negotiated unseen 16 cm step-downs and crossed five outdoor terrains. The policy was trained exclusively on flat ground in simulation with at most 3 kg of added mass.

title: A Benchmark Hit Is Not an Exposure: What Published Vision-Language Geolocation Accuracy Says About Location Privacy, Why One Model Locates 61 Percent of One Photo Set to a Kilometre and Fewer Than 12 Percent of Another to a Hundred, and the Exposure Estimand a Privacy Claim Needs
abstract: (c) 2026 Pranay Mahendrakar. Licensed under CC BY 4.0. Life of Research Since 2024 a growing literature has argued that general-purpose vision-language models can work out where a photograph was taken well enough to make image geolocation an immediate privacy risk, and a second literature has begun building defences against it. In this analysis the author reviews and synthesises published results to show that the direction of that claim survives the evidence but its usual support does not: the accuracies quoted for it are properties of particular photo sets, adversaries and distance thresholds, and none of them is the quantity a privacy claim is about. The same model places 61 percent of a curated, text-rich stock-photo set within one kilometre, about 23 percent of a public Flickr benchmark, and fewer than 12 percent of sampled street-level images within one hundred kilometres. One video-frame benchmark reports 65.6 percent within a kilometre for clips from one platform and 6.4 percent for clips from another. The obvious deflation, that benchmark images were seen in training, does not explain the capability: on photographs collected by the authors and not drawn from any public source, frontier models still name the city about 60 percent of the time, and freshly taken photographs of Seoul are located about as well as Street View images of the same city. The author separates five variables that published results leave unfixed (image population, harm radius, adversary configuration, counterfactual baseline, and the unit of exposure), shows that defences are mostly scored against a fixed adversary although a published photograph must resist every later one, and proposes an exposure protocol that states each variable before a number is reported.

title: When Tools Fail, Agents Fabricate: Silent Failure and Verification-First Oversight in Tool-Using LLM Agents
abstract: Tool-using LLM agents must recover when a tool call fails, by retrying, switching tools, or revising their plan. We study how agents fail when tools fail, using RetryRealistic, a sandboxed yet realistic testbed for controlled fault injection in which agents operate on a real OS filesystem with genuine permission enforcement, SQLite databases, a deterministic local HTTP server, and a constrained shell, across 8 tools, 9 fault types with controlled persistence, and 30 multi-step tasks. Evaluating four agents over 2,100 faulted runs against ground truth, we find that recovery is unreliable (19-68% correct) and frequently silent: 6-26% of runs end in a confident fabrication, a wrong answer asserted as fact. The failure mode is governed more by the fault type than by the model: faults that return partial data drive fabrication (up to 38%), while hard denials drive honest failure. The mechanism is what we call silent ingestion: the agent accepts faulted data as valid on first contact without retrying or flagging the problem, then builds a fabricated answer on top of it. We show that fabrication is reducible: a verification-first Monitor, grounding checks in structured tool outputs and issuing corrective directives rather than hard blocks, raises correct recovery from 45.6% to 56.3% and cuts fabrication from 17.3% to 10.8%. Removing chain-of-thought increases fabrication (+8.3pp), so deliberation guards against silent ingestion. We release RetryRealistic, the fault-injection toolkit, and all annotated traces at https://github.com/Kingsford-Group/RetryRealistic

title: $\varepsilon$-SegFormer: Multi-Resolution Vision Transformers for Sparsely Supervised Segmentation in Electron Microscopy
abstract: Segmenting organelles in electron microscopy (EM) volumes requires dense annotations that take experts months to produce, and every gain in imaging resolution adds to this cost. Sparsely supervised methods reduce this cost to a small fraction of labeled pixels, but the convolutional networks they build on see a limited neighborhood around each pixel, while the identity of an organelle often depends on context far beyond it. We introduce $\varepsilon$-SegFormer, a multi-resolution Vision Transformer for sparsely supervised semantic segmentation, which builds on the architecture of MuViT and extends the training method of $\varepsilon$-Seg. For each labeled pixel, $\varepsilon$-SegFormer samples views at three physical resolutions centered on it, embeds their patches into a single token sequence, and encodes every token's position in image coordinates, so that attention relates all views in one shared frame. A segmentation head classifies the pixel from the tokens around it; during training, the pixel's own token is hidden, so the label must be predicted from context rather than local appearance. The model is trained in a single stage, without pretraining, with an auxiliary reconstruction loss. On the BetaSeg FIB-SEM dataset, $\varepsilon$-SegFormer learns from about 10,000 labeled pixels among the 670 million voxels inside three cells, and, given the cell mask, segments nuclei, mitochondria and insulin granules in a slice of a fourth, unseen cell with an average Dice of 0.89 (0.91 after post-processing). Ablations show that coarser views improve accuracy and that a compact head on local tokens works best, with the wider context entering through attention in the encoder.

title: Turnout: Adaptive Attention Switching for Efficient Reasoning
abstract: Post-hoc transformer linearization replaces the key-value cache of full attention, which grows linearly with generation length, with a fixed size state. This change reduces memory consumption but often hurts accuracy. In reasoning tasks, which require long generations, this effect is especially pronounced. In this work we introduce Turnout, a method that mitigates accuracy loss as a result of linearization, while maintaining its memory-reduction benefits. We apply post-hoc linearization to a pretrained full-attention model, training a linear path through distillation while leaving the original full-attention path unchanged. During response generation, the resulting hybrid model retains both paths and uses a learned policy to control when each layer switches from full to linear attention. We train the policy with reinforcement learning using a reward that balances answer correctness and memory use. Empirical evaluation of our method shows that the learned adaptive policy achieves a better accuracy-efficiency Pareto frontier on reasoning tasks compared to fixed switching and static hybrid baselines.

title: LongCat Recall Sparse Attention: Co-Designing Key Organization and Retrieval for Long-Context Inference
abstract: Retrieval-based sparse attention, exemplified by DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA), reduces attention computation by selecting a small subset of key-value entries. However, selecting these entries can still require searching the entire visible history. For long sequences, retrieval becomes a major bottleneck, limiting the efficiency gains from sparse attention. To address this problem, we propose LongCat Recall Sparse Attention (LRSA), which combines fine-grained representatives with paged retrieval in an incrementally maintained index. LRSA partitions the sequence into time buckets that can be indexed independently as new keys arrive, without regrouping existing history. Within each bucket, it organizes indexing keys into capacity-balanced directional groups and packs a fixed number of complete groups into each page, retaining a separate center for every group. These centers provide fine-grained representatives for page selection, after which refinement scores members of the selected pages together with sink, sliding-window, and visible unindexed candidates to select the final Top-$K$ logical positions. To execute this retrieval process efficiently, we store members in reordered pages, fuse construction stages according to group size, and share storage for overlapping fixed candidates across queries during chunked prefill. These choices support regular member access while reducing kernel launches during construction and repeated candidate transfers. Moreover, we integrate LRSA into SGLang to maintain the index during inference, overlapping asynchronous index construction for new buckets with subsequent computation and reusing compatible bucket indices and member pages after a prefix match in the original key-value pool. With a 1024K-token context, LRSA accelerates key selection by 4.70$\times$ over DSA and combined selection and attention by 35.60$\times$ over full attention.

title: Rethinking Cross-Sensor Domain Adaptation for Bridge Point Cloud Semantic Segmentation
abstract: Segmentation models for bridge point clouds lose accuracy when trained on terrestrial laser scanning (TLS) data and applied to mobile laser scanning (MLS) data. This study re-examines the SemanticBridge TLS-to-MLS protocol to determine how sampling density, surface roughness, color, and acquisition viewpoint are expressed in the 8-cm sparse-voxel representation, and how adaptation gains depend on source-model convergence. Using one sparse-convolution U-Net, we combine raw-point statistics with controlled input perturbations and compare adaptive batch normalization, entropy minimization, Mean Teacher, and confidence-filtered self-training under 100- and 300-epoch schedules. TLS and MLS have similar nearest-neighbor spacing after preprocessing (12.08 and 12.02 mm), and a 4-mm perturbation of TLS points changes voxel occupancy by only 4.4%. Color distributions differ systematically, but zeroing color on identical voxels changes target mean intersection over union (mIoU) by only +0.02, and by +0.06 after the color augmentation is scale-corrected. The sensors also observe different portions of the bridge, yielding different class proportions. A 300-epoch source-only model obtains 57.80 mIoU on the paired-bridge protocol. Confidence-filtered self-training improves the 100-epoch baseline, but from a converged model it changes target mIoU by -0.97 (source-selected checkpoints) and -2.44 (final-50-epoch means). Repeated evaluation (standard deviation 0.27-0.64) and seed variation (1.88 across three seeds) are comparable to several method differences. Adaptation results on this benchmark therefore depend on representation scale, source-model convergence, and evaluation variability.

title: Alignment under Hard Negative Re-Pairing: Cross-Modal Similarity, Scale and Retrieval
abstract: Do vision and language models represent the world alike? That question hides three: what structure each modality has, whether the two modalities organize images and their captions alike, and whether a model ranks an image's own caption highly. Centered kernel alignment (CKA) and neighborhood agreement answer the second, yet matching and model selection use them as if they identified individual pairs and answered the third. To test this reading, we introduce hard negative re-pairing: every image receives the caption of a similar image, and nothing else changes. Although no image keeps its own caption and annotators judge a majority of the substituted captions wrong, CKA stays higher than under a random re-pairing that keeps 80% of the original pairs. In all 22 image-text models we test, neighborhood agreement loses far less than top-one retrieval, which collapses. The reason is scale: these diagnostics pool over many neighbors, matching and retrieval are decided among the nearest ones, and an exact decomposition shows that near-neighbor pairs contribute almost nothing to CKA. In the matching problems we test, an exact maximizer of CKA would not return the original pairing. On COCO and Flickr30k, the model with the highest diagnostic value retrieves worse on held-out data than the model chosen by validation recall, even where the two correlate positively. What re-pairing removes is the informative part: that share tracks retrieval on both datasets and ranks encoder pairs before alignment training. A diagnostic should be reported with its question and its scale, and tested against hard negative re-pairing.

title: Energy-preserving Bayesian model reduction: closed-form structured posteriors and probabilistic stability certificates for quadratic operator inference
abstract: Bayesian operator inference learns reduced-order models (ROMs) with polynomial structure from state data and returns a closed-form Gaussian posterior over the reduced operators. That posterior is unconstrained, so it gives positive probability to operators with unbounded dynamics, and current practice controls this only through finite-horizon simulation tests on a few samples. We show that energy preservation of the quadratic operator is a set of linear equality constraints, which can be imposed exactly inside the Bayesian formulation without losing the closed form. In particular, the constrained posterior follows from one Kalman-type update of the unconstrained one, and its samples are obtained exactly, by the same correction applied to unconstrained draws. Under this structure, global boundedness for all initial conditions and bounded inputs reduces to a linear matrix condition on the symmetric part of the linear operator. The simulation test is then replaced by a probabilistic stability certificate: the posterior probability that the ROM is globally bounded, estimated with exact confidence bounds; the posterior restricted to certified models is then sampled exactly by rejection. For energy-conserving systems, the linear part can be constrained to be skew-symmetric as well: every draw then grows at most linearly in time, and conserves energy exactly when unforced. On a forced viscous Burgers' equation, the Korteweg-de Vries equation and a two-dimensional viscous Burgers' equation, every sample of the constrained posterior integrates to a bounded trajectory, where up to all unconstrained draws diverge, and beyond the observation window the former is also the more accurate of the two.

title: Constraint-Aware Anticlustering Decomposition for Certifying Pairwise-Constrained Clustering
abstract: Certifying the quality of feasible solutions to large-scale minimum sum-of-squares clustering with pairwise must-link and cannot-link constraints remains challenging, as it requires strong lower bounds on the optimal objective value. We propose a decomposition framework that partitions the data points into smaller subsets, called anticlusters, and solves the induced clustering subproblems to obtain a certified optimality gap for the original problem. To preserve pairwise information, we introduce the Constrained Anticlustering Problem (CAP), which assigns each connected component of the constraint graph to a single anticluster while seeking geometrically representative subsets. We formulate CAP as a mixed-integer second-order cone program and develop a variable neighborhood search heuristic to construct high-quality decompositions. The resulting lower bound remains valid even when the induced subproblems are not solved to global optimality. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets with up to approximately 4,000 observations show that our approach can achieve mean optimality gaps below 1% at a modest computational cost.

title: NightmareDiscourseBench: A Benchmark Dataset for Fictional Direct Discourse Identification Pipelines
abstract: In this paper we introduce a new benchmark dataset, NightmareDiscourseBench, for testing NLP pipelines that identify forms of direct discourse in English-language fiction. We first review existing publicly available benchmarks (providing summary statistics and reviewing available metadata) for this task, identifying theoretical inconsistency and exclusive focus on speech as primary issues in this domain. We then overview our narrative theory-based framework for classifying and evaluating different forms of direct discourse, and finally describe NightmareDiscourseBench, a new benchmark test set of 12 text samples accompanied by metadata pertinent to the task of direct discourse identification.

title: TabK: Amortized Bayesian Estimation of the Number of Clusters in Tabular Data
abstract: Estimating the number of clusters, $k$, is a fundamental prerequisite for most clustering algorithms. Traditionally, this estimation has relied on computationally expensive grid searches over internal cluster validity indices (CVIs) or adaptive clustering algorithms, both constrained by specific statistical assumptions. We introduce TabK, a zero-shot, permutation-invariant transformer architecture that frames the estimation of $k$ as an amortized Bayesian inference problem for tabular data. TabK leverages a novel Quantile Feature Encoder (QFE) to extract position-free, content-derived representations from empirical marginal distributions. title: From Point Clouds to Engineering Models: Benchmarking Agentic 3D Reconstruction in the Built Environment
abstract: Coding agents can translate 3D measurements into CAD geometry, but reconstructing engineering models for the built environment demands semantic interpretation and consistent construction constraints beyond surface fitting. We formulate scene-level Scan-to-BIM (Building Information Modeling) as an agentic 3D coding task and introduce S2Bench, comprising public and proprietary scans of 128 real-world scenes across five domains, paired with expert-curated reference models spanning diverse spatial scales. A shared framework lets agents measure scans in Python, build class-labeled components in a live CAD/BIM kernel, and iteratively refine their code. We also propose parallel asynchronous collaboration, where a lead delegates versioned tasks, continues modeling while workers execute, and integrates revision-bound proposals. Evaluating five agents and a collaborative team across 1,028 reconstructions shows that scan-to-model residuals directly guide geometric repair, whereas inferring semantic classes and construction relations requires joint geometric, visual, and engineering reasoning that agents struggle to ground and verify. Consequently, the leading agent fits scan geometry closely ($96\%$ coverage within $5\,\text{cm}$) yet reaches only $63\%$ mIoU, and no agent passes all engineering checks on more than $38\%$ of scenes. Coverage and engineering conformance drop with scene scale, whereas running a smaller model as a team improves all three axes with greater coverage gains on larger scenes. The project page is available at https://tumcms.github.io/S2Bench.github.io/

title: Trained on Harm, Still Refusing: A Training-Time Defense for Code Generation
abstract: Fine-tuning enables safety-aligned code language models to adapt to diverse downstream tasks. However, training on untrusted data can severely undermine their ability to refuse harmful requests. Notably, we find that models comply with harmful requests even though harmfulness information remains highly decodable from their internal representations. Moreover, an initial preference for refusal does not necessarily translate into sustained refusal behavior throughout generation. Together, these findings reveal a critical gap between recognizing harmful requests and consistently refusing to fulfill them. To address this gap, we introduce SAFEHOLD, a novel provider-enforced defense framework that preserves safety alignment during harmful fine-tuning by treating refusal as a sustained generation process rather than a single response decision. Specifically, SAFEHOLD preserves the aligned model's full-vocabulary response distribution at the initial generation position through decision-boundary anchoring, while supervising the complete refusal sequence through refusal-path reinforcement. We conduct extensive experiments evaluating safety, utility, and internal mechanisms. SAFEHOLD reduces average ASR by 72.03 percentage points relative to undefended fine-tuning, outperforming five SOTA defenses by 24.32 to 70.87 percentage points. Meanwhile, it improves average HumanEval pass@1 by 10.24 percentage points over undefended fine-tuning, while maintaining an average XSTest over-refusal rate of only 2.73 percent. Overall, these results demonstrate that SAFEHOLD effectively mitigates safety degradation during harmful fine-tuning while preserving benign-task utility.

title: CreditFilter: Calibrated Token Weights over the Within-Response Entropy Rank for RLVR
abstract: Critic-free reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) typically assigns a uniform advantage to every token. Token-reweighting heuristics like the 80/20 mask favor high-entropy tokens, but fail to measure a token's actual impact on the outcome. We formalize this impact as the forking value: the variance of the success probability over the policy's next-token choices. The expected forking values along a response sum exactly to the reward variance. Token credit is thus, in expectation over a prompt's responses, a fixed budget spent at the forks. This motivates weights that redistribute credit within a response. The forking value factorizes into a fork consequence, which requires costly continuations to estimate, and a fork probability, which the softmax provides. On Qwen3-8B-Base, this fork probability decays exponentially with a token's within-response entropy rank at class-specific rates, revealing that most tokens carry negligible forking value. CreditFilter weights each token by an exponential window over the same rank. The window is calibrated to this fork-probability envelope, under an approximately flat fork consequence. CreditFilter needs no extra forward passes and is stabilized by difficulty damping and an entropy-gated fallback. Averaged over three seeds, it outperforms DAPO by 7.7 points on MATH500 and by 10.5 and 9.1 points on AIME24 and AIME25. Its dynamically adaptive variant matches it. The ablations show that both parts matter: ranking tokens within each response rather than across the batch, and matching the window's decay rate to the envelope. Code is available at https://github.com/yoctta/CreditFilter.

title: Structural Agreement Indicates Prediction Accuracy For Protein-Ligand Co-Folding
abstract: Co-folding models predict the structures of proteins and their bound ligands, but their accuracy varies across targets. Their usefulness therefore depends on knowing which predictions a user can trust. Confidence scores are intended to guide that choice. However, across seven co-folding models, we show that confidence-based selection offers little improvement over choosing a prediction at random. For approximately three-quarters of structures, predictions are either exclusively correct or incorrect, leaving no opportunity for ranking to change the outcome. Moreover, high confidence does not reliably discriminate correct top-ranked predictions from incorrect ones. We find that structural agreement among predictions is a more accurate measure of likely success than current confidence scores. We capture this with the Concentration of Repeated Ensembles (CORE) Score, which combines cluster tightness with ensemble support. CORE Score discriminates top-1 success and oracle success, achieving mean ROC AUCs of 0.866 and 0.838, compared to 0.757 and 0.759 for ipTM. CORE Score also outperforms training set similarity measures, including ligand Tanimoto, protein sequence, and Runs N' Poses similarity, despite requiring no experimental ligand pose. Structural agreement is therefore a practical indicator of reliability and a baseline for evaluating future confidence estimators, without requiring an additional trained uncertainty estimator.

title: GlaucomaMarker - Biomarker-Grounded Glaucoma Vision-Language Model
abstract: Glaucoma is a leading cause of irreversible blindness. In the current clinical setting, glaucoma diagnosis is generally conducted by assessing optic disc cupping and asymmetry. Vision-language models (VLMs) have been utilized in recent years for glaucoma, mostly trained on fixed templates or AI-generated captions, as no public text describes the biomarkers. Our proposed framework, GlaucomaMarker, hypothesizes that retinal structural biomarkers can ground glaucoma-based VLMs. It converts public segmentation masks into sentences describing eleven biomarkers, to teach retinal foundation models to read them. We applied this framework to RETFound (GlaucomaMarker-R) and FLAIR (GlaucomaMarker-F), training on 9,778 images that yielded 45,190 image-text pairs. On a real-world clinical cohort, GlaucomaMarker-F detects glaucoma with an AUROC of 0.905, against 0.848 for FLAIR, and both read the biomarkers where baselines stay near random guessing. Since the biomarker text is computed from existing masks, it comes at no extra cost.

title: Feasibility of Multifrequency Neural Network-Based Wave Inversion in Ultrasound Time-Harmonic Elastography
abstract: Ultrasound time-harmonic elastography (THE) is a non-invasive imaging technique that measures soft-tissue stiffness. Relying on the same principle of time-harmonic shear wave excitation as established magnetic resonance elastography (MRE), THE offers full field-of-view stiffness mapping at short acquisition times and sub-second temporal resolution across organs. However, reconstruction of shear wave speed maps from acquired tissue wavefields remains challenging due to speckle noise and sparse spatial coverage of the lateral component. Deep learning methods have shown promising results for image reconstruction in transient-based ultrasound elastography modalities but remain unexplored in THE. In MRE, MF-ElastoNet, a 2D multifrequency neural network-based wave reconstruction method trained on synthetic physics-based wave data, has shown high generalizability across dynamic ranges and resolutions. We investigated the potential of a multifrequency neural network-based wave inversion for THE, by performing a first feasibility analysis. To this end, we adapted the processing pipeline of MF-ElastoNet from MRE to THE. We tested our approach on THE acquired phantom data from the algorithms for mapping elastic modulus Challenge, as well as on in vivo liver THE in 4 healthy volunteers and 14 patients with focal liver lesions, including benign focal nodular hyperplasia, and malignant hepatocellular carcinoma and adenocarcinoma. MF-ElastoNet was successfully adapted to THE with in vivo liver testing. Compared with k-MDEV, the state-of-the-art wave inversion method for THE, Bland-Altman analysis showed a mean bias of -0.02 m/s (95% limits of agreement: -0.36 to 0.33 m/s).

title: EAST: Event-Anchored Surface Transport for Event-Based Gaussian Reconstruction
abstract: Event-supervised Gaussian reconstruction combines the high temporal resolution and wide dynamic range of event cameras with efficient explicit rendering. However, recovering a continuous surface remains difficult: changes in rendered appearance can compensate for depth errors while preserving the predicted brightness changes. We introduce Event-Anchored Surface Transport (EAST), which couples an event-constrained signed distance field to Gaussian rendering. Triangulation-supported candidates anchor the zero set, while normal flow measured from event timing constrains ray-surface intersection depths. Gaussian centers receive bounded corrections from the descriptor difference between the live field and a frozen initial reference. The correction is zero at initialization, yet transmits image gradients to the live field. Experiments on PAEv3D and NeRF Synthetic show improved surface accuracy and reference-view rendering over Gaussian baselines, together with efficient mesh extraction from the learned field.

title: Learning 3D MRI Representations with Generative Adversarial Networks
abstract: Learning representations of visual images is a challenging task. It requires extracting abstract patterns from high-dimensional data without explicit supervision. This becomes pronounced with 3D MR imaging due to sparse features, higher dimensional inputs, and smaller datasets. Many state-of-the-art representation learning algorithms successfully rely on transformers and diffusion-based architectures. However, these methods struggle with smaller datasets. In effect, solution methods relax the problem by slicing 3D volumes and solving the problem for 2D medical imaging, resulting in a loss of spatial 3D information. We present R2RG, a representation learning method based on Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), with Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) honing the reconstruction task. Our key insights lie in exploiting architectural biases in 3D CNNs, combined with data-efficient auto-encoding GANs and a composite loss function to enhance reconstruction fidelity and stabilize training. Our experiments on three standard datasets and a locally collected dataset show that R2RG not only achieves superior performance but also generalizes to heterogeneous and smaller datasets. Furthermore, representations learned with R2RG outperform those learned with contrastive-based representation learning methods on Parkinson's and Alzheimer's disease classification. Our work demonstrates that reconstruction-based representation learning is a promising direction for 3D medical imaging under limited data availability.

title: Decision models for UAVBench and the viability of edge deployment
abstract: Small language models are often proposed for reasoning onboard a drone. However, a good benchmark score does not tell us whether a model will actually run, and run usefully, on an edge computer. In this paper we study three related questions using the UAV decision benchmark, UAVBench. First, are small structured decision models good candidates for these tasks? Second, can an ordinary local machine (a Mac) screen candidate models before we test them on physical devices? Third, what software and resource limits govern deployment? Our main Mac evaluation covers 24 model configurations on the same 2,000 validated multiple-choice questions from UAVBench. These include 20 size-and-precision configurations of 11 generative models, plus four open-weight structured decision models that received no additional UAVBench-specific training. A structured decision model, H2O Lightning 4B, achieved the highest accuracy we observed, scoring 77.65% on the Mac. This shows that these models are well suited to this kind of task. However, when we tried to deploy the decision models, we ran into conversion and runtime limits on the edge devices we tested, which we describe in detail. To test local screening, we ran matched evaluations of two generative models on both the Mac and a Qualcomm RB3 board. The accuracies did not match exactly, but the ranking did. LFM2 2.6B ranked above Qwen2.5 1.5B on both platforms. This supports using a local machine to shortlist candidates. That said, individual answers still differed between platforms, so testing on the actual hardware remained necessary.

title: When Does Looking Closer Pay Off? Simple Foveated ViTs for Fine-Grained Recognition
abstract: Fine-grained recognition benefits from high resolution, but not every image region needs it. We study a foveated Vision Transformer (FoVT) that uses last-block class attention from a 224-pixel glance to select regions for refinement. Fine patches from the 448-pixel image replace the selected coarse cells, and the same backbone classifies the mixed-resolution input. We evaluate FoVT on five benchmarks with two seeds and 26 configurations per dataset. Attention beats random selection on all five benchmarks, by up to 2.45 percentage points overall and 4.18 points on the smallest objects. At equal transformer cost, Holm-corrected tests detect no FoVT deficit relative to a port of the official CF-ViT, but no dataset shows a corrected FoVT advantage in both seeds. FoVT requires no feature reuse, distillation loss, or selection schedule. Reusing coarse features shows no significant benefit and costs 1 to 3 points when the reuse module is trained at the head learning rate. Skipping refinement for the most confident 19 to 24 percent of images leaves accuracy unchanged to two decimal places. At the transformer cost of uniform 336-pixel inference, gated FoVT improves accuracy on four benchmarks, with the largest gains on NABirds and FGVC-Aircraft and no significant gain on Stanford Dogs. Foveation primarily saves computation: relative to a uniform 448-pixel model trained with the same auxiliary glance loss, ungated FoVT uses 44 percent fewer transformer operations, with no significant accuracy difference on four benchmarks and a 0.53-point deficit on FGVC-Aircraft. Wall-clock savings are smaller than the reduction in transformer operations.

title: Learning Unknown Oscillators From Bandit Feedback
abstract: We study semi-bandits driven by unknown oscillators. Each round, a learner selects two of four reward channels and observes their individual rewards. Frequency errors change future reward rankings and the resulting measurements. We show when committing to one fitted oscillator lets its greedy choices expose prediction errors. Our controller bounds reward loss (regret) over a continuous confidence set and holds the longest block within budget. An online regression policy gathers observations when the check fails. Regret grows at a square-root rate, up to logarithmic factors, across all frequencies and extends to two competing oscillators. On 96 fresh synthetic instances, checked commitment uses 49 fits instead of 1,023, with 1.5% higher mean regret than fitting every round. Matched isolated timings give a 4.69-fold speedup. The confidence sets also certify trajectory regret.

title: LiDAR Signals for Robot Locomotion: Spherical Range Images Enable Robust Sim-to-Real Transfer
abstract: Existing legged-locomotion systems commonly rely on depth images or online elevation maps. However, depth-based policies suffer from perceptual sim-to-real discrepancies due to imperfect depth sensor modeling, while map-based approaches are vulnerable to drift and misalignment. LiDAR offers direct measurements of the surrounding geometry, but raw LiDAR scans lack a compact, structured representation for high-frequency control. We propose a LiDAR perception pipeline that maintains perceptual consistency across simulation and reality through sensing- and representation-level alignment. At the sensor level, we recover frame-wise angular sampling patterns from the physical LiDAR and replay them in simulation with GPU ray casting. At the representation level, simulated and real returns undergo the same spherical range image encoding, yielding a fixed-size policy observation for end-to-end training and direct deployment without teacher--student distillation, online elevation mapping, or adaptation. Experiments show that our range-image policies achieve stronger sim-to-real transfer than depth- and elevation-map-based baselines, while ablations confirm the importance of the proposed sensing components. More visualizations and real-world videos are available at the \href{https://lidar-img.github.io/}

evidence.abstract: Existing legged-locomotion systems commonly rely on depth images or online elevation maps. However, depth-based policies suffer from perceptual sim-to-real discrepancies due to imperfect depth sensor modeling, while map-based approaches are vulnerable to drift and misalignment. LiDAR offers direct measurements of the surrounding geometry, but raw LiDAR scans lack a compact, structured representation for high-frequency control. We propose a LiDAR perception pipeline that maintains perceptual consistency across simulation and reality through sensing- and representation-level alignment. At the sensor level, we recover frame-wise angular sampling patterns from the physical LiDAR and replay them in simulation with GPU ray casting. At the representation level, simulated and real returns undergo the same spherical range image encoding, yielding a fixed-size policy observation for end-to-end training and direct deployment without teacher--student distillation, online elevation mapping, or adaptation. Experiments show that our range-image policies achieve stronger sim-to-real transfer than depth- and elevation-map-based baselines, while ablations confirm the importance of the proposed sensing components. More visualizations and real-world videos are available at the \href{https://lidar-img.github.io/}

title: A Continuous Relaxation of Quantization-Aware Training
abstract: Quantization is a critical piece of the deployment pipeline in the era of large generative models. Low-bit quantization, particularly 2-bits or sub-2-bits, is a notoriously difficult problem, particularly when using a channelwise quantization scheme which has been shown as a leading candidate for hardware-efficiency. The key challenges with low-bit quantization range from limited quantization levels to saddle points or flat regions in the loss surface. In this paper, we look at the problem of flat quantization loss surfaces through a lens of dynamically changing bitwidth. Unlike existing techniques which either change the bit-precision abruptly or keep it fixed, we propose to gradually alter the bitwidth as the model trains. To this end, we propose RelaxQAT, a continuous relaxation of the QAT process. We also provide simple theoretical and empirical insights behind why RelaxQAT helps the QAT performance. Our extensive experiments demonstrate up to 6.3% average accuracy gains on vision and up to 7.7% better average accuracy on natural language tasks, compared to the leading QAT methods.

title: AV-FLARE: Feature-Level Reliability Estimation for Multimodal Emotion Recognition
abstract: Multimodal emotion recognition (MMER) systems typically rely on learned feature representations and attention mechanisms that implicitly weight information across time and modalities. However, these mechanisms do not explicitly incorporate input reliability, despite the presence of noise in audio, occlusions in visual data, and the sparse and event-driven nature of affective cues. We propose AV-FLARE, a framework that explicitly estimates fine-grained reliability scores across both temporal and feature dimensions prior to temporal modeling and uses them to modulate feature representations. Reliability is computed using two complementary components: (i) a supervised network trained jointly with the classification objective, and (ii) an unsupervised Gaussian Mixture Model that models global feature distributions. These signals are combined to provide both task-driven and distribution-aware reliability estimates. To integrate modalities, we introduce a hierarchical cross-modal attention mechanism in which textual features are used to guide audio-visual fusion as a semantic reference modality. Experiments on the IEMOCAP dataset show that AV-FLARE improves over a no-reliability baseline, achieving 90.81\% accuracy and 81.69\% F1-score, corresponding to gains of +4.41% and +8.56%, respectively. These results suggest that incorporating explicit input reliability estimation may improve robustness in multimodal emotion recognition under the evaluated setting.

title: Neural Defend ARCAS 290M: A Robust Foundation Model for AI-Generated Audio Detection
abstract: Voice cloning now needs only seconds of audio, and detectors tuned to one dataset often fail when the generator, channel, or language changes. We introduce ARCAS 290M, Neural Defend's foundation model for detecting AI-generated audio. A single frozen production model, with no benchmark-specific fine-tuning, generalizes across text-to-speech, voice-conversion, and codec-language-model generators, telephone and Bluetooth channels, recording conditions, and languages. We evaluate it on the complete official test sets of ten public benchmarks, scoring every recording exactly as released, and against commercial systems on independent leaderboards. ARCAS 290M ranks first among all systems on the Podonos leaderboard and has the lowest equal error rate among commercial detectors on ASVspoof5. It separates real from AI-generated speech almost perfectly on ASVspoof5, SpeechFake, and ShiftySpeech, and detects nearly all AI-generated speech in Hindi, Tamil, Bengali, and Telugu. On every benchmark with a published zero-shot comparison, including in-the-wild audio, partial fakes, and the conditions hardest for the field, it surpasses the strongest reported detector by a wide margin. These results establish ARCAS 290M as a general-purpose foundation for AI-generated audio detection in fraud prevention, platform safety, and media verification.

title: Alignment without Transfer: Tokenization Impacts Cross-lingual Representations during Multilingual Language Model Pretraining
abstract: Tokenization represents one of the most crucial steps in mulilingual NLP pipelines. Yet, tokenizers routinely under-allocate vocabulary to low-resource languages. While improved allocation leads to better performance, it remains poorly understood how tokenization shapes cross-lingual representations and transfer during pretraining. To address this, we pretrain 39 mono- and bilingual 1B decoder-only models on FineWeb2-HQ across English, German, French, Arabic and Chinese, varying only the tokenizer. Our results demonstrate that improved vocabulary allocation (i) substantially raises cross-lingual representation alignment in early-to-mid layers, an effect that prior work measuring only the output layer could not observe, (ii) increases cross-lingual parametric knowledge sharing in feed-forward neurons, supported by correlational and causal evidence, and (iii) an alignment-transfer dissociation, where cross-lingual transfer remains essentially unchanged despite higher alignment. Moreover, transfer is significantly lower for cross-script bilinguals even under fair vocabulary allocation, indicating that the script barrier is not merely a tokenizer artifact. All of our checkpoints and code are publicly available.

title: Bel: Step-Level Policy Improvement of Visual Agents Without Training
abstract: A visual agent acts on what it sees: it taps and types on a screen, or points on a camera image to show a robot where to act. One wrong step can fail its task, yet the right action is often among its own samples, passed over by its greedy decode. Choosing it is a visual judgment, since an action is best judged where it acts, not by its text or coordinates alone: as text, a tap is two numbers; drawn on the screen, it is the Post button of an empty draft. We find that this is decisive: given the screenshot and a tap's coordinates, a decision model chooses among GUI-R1-3B's samples significantly worse on average than when the tap is drawn where it lands. Bel turns this finding into a method that trains nothing and needs only a frozen policy's samples and an image on which each action can be drawn. It marks each candidate on its own copy of the image it acts on, asks a decision model for the probability that executing it is the right decision, so that every kind of action shares one scale, and acts on another candidate only when greedy scores below a threshold and trails it by a margin. On recorded GUI steps, for each of three policies, Bel significantly beats greedy decoding on mobile, web and desktop screens alike and, on the same candidates, gives each a significantly higher mean step success than voting, CATTS, the trained GUI-Critic-R1 and two prompted Qwen3-VL judges shown the same marks; it also significantly improves the much larger Qwen3-VL-235B-A22B on every step-level test set. With GUI-R1-3B's thresholds unchanged, Bel significantly raises live AndroidWorld and MiniWoB++ task success for two other policies and robot-pointing success for three policies on each of two groups of benchmarks. Judging each action where it acts thus gives step-level policy improvement of visual agents without training, with significant gains for GUI agents and robot pointing.

title: Isolating the Language Shell: A Content-Controlled Study of Multilingual Reasoning
abstract: Multilingual reasoning distillation requires choosing the language in which teacher reasoning is presented, yet existing recipes often entangle linguistic form with differences in generation, translation, and filtering. We construct content-controlled supervision by rendering the same verified English trajectories into English, translated target-language, and language-mixed shells, and fine-tune two pretrained students in three target languages, evaluating them on multilingual mathematical reasoning at two difficulty levels. Even with the underlying reasoning content held fixed, we find that shell choice can change downstream accuracy, with effects varying across students, languages, and difficulty levels. Pre-training compatibility does not consistently track these outcomes, and even when our tests find no clear accuracy difference between shells, their output-language behavior can still differ substantially. These results suggest that the supervision shell is a distinct design choice in multilingual reasoning distillation.

title: Coarse-to-Fine Dyadic Sampling: An Exact First-Hit Result and an Exploratory QAOA Benchmark
abstract: This preprint introduces two deterministic coarse-to-fine dyadic sampling strategies and presents an exact first-hit expectation for contiguous target regions, supported by Lean formal verification. Their application to QAOA parameter optimization is explored through reproducible MaxCut simulations and comparisons with classical optimization methods. The results highlight potential applications, limitations, and directions for further research.

title: MatHarness: Towards Long-Horizon Open-ended AutoResearch for Computational Materials Science
abstract: Materials science research is a non-linear, long-horizon process. Existing scientific agents, however, largely rely on specific task execution or predefined workflows, rendering them brittle in open-ended settings. To bridge this gap, we present MatHarness, an agent harness designed for open-ended, long-horizon computational materials research spanning the complete lifecycle from initial ideation to manuscript writing. MatHarness couples three mechanisms: execution robustness through pre-flight verification, expert-distilled skills, and just-in-time auditing; epistemic adaptability through persistent research artifacts and an evolving scientific mental model; and collective intelligence through a heterogeneous multi-agent round table under targeted human oversight. We evaluate MatHarness on adsorbate-induced surface segregation in Cu-Zn alloys, an open question in methanol-synthesis catalysis. Over a multi-week trajectory consuming roughly 10^3 GPU-hours (50 production DFT relaxations prescreened by 171 machine-learning-potential evaluations) the system revised its plan six times, recovered autonomously from failed calculations, and had an independent auditor overturn one of its own over-attributed claims before publication. Within the sampled metallic dilute-limit models, the validated DFT analysis supports an adsorbate-induced tendency toward greater surface Cu exposure at both composition endpoints, with facet- and coverage-dependent exceptions. These results were compiled into a complete manuscript with human involvement concentrated in specification, approval, and strategic steering gates. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/PrentisAI/pippin.

title: A Benchmark Protocol and Fairness Analysis Towards Open-Set EEG Seizure Type Classification
abstract: Automated EEG seizure type classification systems are typically trained and evaluated under the closed-set assumption, where all seizure types encountered at deployment are seen during training. In clinical practice, this assumption fails: patients present with rare or atypical seizure types that fall outside the training label space, and a system that forces a wrong label is worse than one that abstains. We introduce the first open-set recognition protocol for EEG seizure type classification on the Temple University Hospital Seizure Corpus (TUSZ v2.0.3), defining known and unknown classes using the clinical taxonomy itself: seizure types with sufficient subject representation (at least 12 subjects) form the known set, and rare types form the unknown set. We evaluate seven post-hoc open-set scorers (MSP, MaxLogit, energy, Mahalanobis, kNN, GHOST, and COSTARR) applied to a partially fine-tuned EEG Foundation Model (EFM), using a subject-disjoint leave-one-class-out (LOCO) protocol over three seeds that tests whether methods can detect seizure types excluded from fine-tuning. On true unknown classes, the best scorer (Mahalanobis) reaches a mean AUROC of 0.66, and differences among the top scorers are within seed-to-seed variation. Held-out known seizure types from unseen subjects are detected only slightly above chance (AUROC 0.54-0.58 for all scorers). Per-subject rejection rates are highly uneven for all scorers, and GHOST does not significantly improve per-subject fairness over energy scoring (two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank, p >= 0.25). We release the protocol, subject splits, and code as an initial baseline; our results indicate that open-set seizure type recognition remains a hard, open problem.

title: NavTTT: Adaptive Parametric Memory via Hierarchical Test-Time Training for Vision-and-Language Navigation
abstract: Vision-and-language navigation (VLN) demands that agents accumulate and reason over streaming visual observations throughout long navigation episodes. Existing approaches struggle to maintain long-term history, constrained by the finite context capacity of transformer architectures. To solve the problem, fast-weight test-time training (TTT) provides a mechanism for encoding streaming observations into an evolving parameter state. However, existing TTT does not distinguish informative observations from repetitive visual content, allowing redundant tokens to interfere with the retention of information needed for subsequent decisions. We propose Navigation-Conditioned Test-Time Training (NavTTT), which introduces adaptive memory formation and hierarchical memory integration for vision-and-language navigation. NavTTT leverages global navigation context to prioritize informative visual evidence and integrates language instructions with spatial information to construct spatially grounded memory representations. Episode-local nonlinear fast weights store these representations as Adaptive Parametric Memory (APM), preserving history beyond the visual context for later decisions. To reduce cross-layer coupling in memory formation, NavTTT maintains independent fast-weight memories across multiple decoder depths. This decoupled design prevents errors or biases from spreading across different memory levels. Meanwhile, it enables shared historical information to be independently represented at various levels of abstraction. Experiments demonstrate strong navigation performance on VLN-CE benchmarks and effective instruction following on a real robot.
