title: Towards Text-Mask Consistency in Medical Image Segmentation
abstract: Vision-language models for medical image segmentation often produce masks that conflict with the accompanying text, especially under multi-site/multi-lesion descriptions. We trace this failure to two factors: (i) highly templated and repetitive clinical language causes one-to-one hard contrastive learning to yield numerous false negatives, weakening cross-modal alignment; and (ii) predominantly vision-driven, one-way cross-attention lacks a language-dominant, spatially aware pathway, hindering effective injection of textual semantics into the spatial visual domain. To this end, we propose Consistency-enhanced Two-stage Segmentation (C2Seg). In the pretraining stage, Cluster-aware Contrastive Learning uses a frozen strong baseline to construct an intra-batch text similarity matrix as soft labels, thereby alleviating false negative conflicts and producing more discriminative visual representations. In the fusion stage, we introduce a Bidirectional Complementary Attention Module, where each modality dominates attention along its own path, fostering deep interaction and structural consistency between visual and textual representations. In order to enhance the expressive power of multimodal features, we further adopt KAN-based Attention Gating. Without updating the language encoder, our approach significantly improves text-mask consistency and segmentation accuracy on four public medical imaging datasets. The source code is available at https://github.com/JGuiidev/C2Seg.

title: Measuring the Generator, Not the State: code, registration and data
abstract: Code, notebooks, dated registration files and data of the article Measuring the Generator, Not the State: The Validity of LLM-Written Negatives for State–Action Scorers (Universidad Autónoma de Ciudad Juárez; submitted to the Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research). The study trains the two heads of a state–action scorer on a frozen Qwen3-8B with 15 training objectives under one protocol, audits the evaluation sets with probes that do not see the state, and measures how the gain from hard negatives written by Gemini transfers to negatives written by a panel of 23 generators. The data are released without any text of Nemotron-CC v2.1, of CLM's negatives or of the generated negatives; data/README.md describes them. Code: Apache License 2.0. Data and documents: CC BY 4.0 (LICENSE-DATA.md).

title: Click and Count: Multimodal Prototype Adaptation for Class-Agnostic Object Counting
abstract: We propose a multimodal, class-agnostic, density-based object counting framework that specifies the object of interest through visual exemplars, a text description, or both, within a single iterative refinement pipeline. Existing counters typically fall into two groups: methods that fuse two modalities, a hand-drawn bounding box and a text description, to specify the target object, and single-modality methods that rely on either a box exemplar or text alone. A few recent methods replace the box with a point or click. We expand a single click into a precise object mask via a frozen visual-prompt segmentation model, feeding an iterative prototype-refinement process that also fuses a text description at every refinement step. We make two contributions: first, a click-derived exemplar extraction module that removes the bounding-box requirement of prior exemplar-based counters; second, a per-step text-fusion mechanism that combines visual and textual prompts throughout refinement. Combined with text guidance, our model achieves state-of-the-art counting accuracy, outperforming prior click-based counting methods across all metrics and surpassing the box-exemplar base architecture in mean absolute error. The code is available at github.com/ameniifi/Click-and-Count.

evidence.title: Click and Count: Multimodal Prototype Adaptation for Class-Agnostic Object Counting
evidence.abstract: We propose a multimodal, class-agnostic, density-based object counting framework that specifies the object of interest through visual exemplars, a text description, or both, within a single iterative refinement pipeline. Existing counters typically fall into two groups: methods that fuse two modalities, a hand-drawn bounding box and a text description, to specify the target object, and single-modality methods that rely on either a box exemplar or text alone. A few recent methods replace the box with a point or click. We expand a single click into a precise object mask via a frozen visual-prompt segmentation model, feeding an iterative prototype-refinement process that also fuses a text description at every refinement step. We make two contributions: first, a click-derived exemplar extraction module that removes the bounding-box requirement of prior exemplar-based counters; second, a per-step text-fusion mechanism that combines visual and textual prompts throughout refinement. Combined with text guidance, our model achieves state-of-the-art counting accuracy, outperforming prior click-based counting methods across all metrics and surpassing the box-exemplar base architecture in mean absolute error. The code is available at github.com/ameniifi/Click-and-Count.

title: Search-RSI: Expanding Search Worlds Along Multimodal Agents' Capability Frontier
abstract: Multimodal search agents answer knowledge intensive visual questions by grounding them in retrieved evidence, and recent recipes train them on multi hop tasks that are synthesized from knowledge graphs and grown online to keep pace with the agent. These recipes, however, treat the searchable world as fixed: a new question can be well formed and verifiable while its evidence is absent from the retrieval backend, so the agent issues the right query, retrieves nothing, and is penalized as if its policy were at fault. Such unreachable negatives accumulate with every round of growth. We propose Search-RSI, a recursive self improvement framework that expands the search world along the agent's capability frontier. In each round, the current policy diagnoses its partially mastered regions of a task space spanned by hop depth, relation rarity, and distractor density; new tasks there are grown together with their evidence; and the same policy decides how they are used: candidates on which its probes disagree feed reinforcement learning, while those beyond its reach become hint guided demonstrations of its own. Keeping the policy inside this loop matters: an improver frozen at the start of training loses 3.2 points. On nine multimodal search benchmarks, Search-RSI keeps improving where static task growth saturates, raising the average accuracy of the recipe it builds on by 9.8 and 9.5 points at 9B and 27B, of which 7.0 points are out of reach for a world that is merely made consistent. The loop uses no external model and only privileged task structure that is removed before training, at 1.27x the compute of static growth.

title: NavRSI: Recursive Harness Self-Improvement for Vision-and-Language Navigation
abstract: Frontier large language models (LLMs) have enabled vision-and-language navigation (VLN) through direct closed-loop perception and action. However, navigation performance depends strongly on the harness governing LLM-environment interactions, while existing harnesses largely rely on manually designed navigation tools, memory, and agent roles. We introduce NavRSI, a harness-centric recursive self-improvement framework that optimizes the navigation behavior of frozen LLMs through closed-loop experience. In each round, NavRSI iteratively collects navigation trajectories and failure diagnostics, employs a designer agent to rewrite the harness, and retains the revisions that prove effective, while the designer accumulates experience from previous revisions so that the harness and this experience co-evolve. Privileged simulator diagnostics guide only the designer and remain inaccessible to the navigating LLM, enabling deployment with a single RGB camera and primitive actions, without task-specific model training or additional navigation tools. Experiments demonstrate consistent improvements across LLMs from four vendors, with 85.64% success rate on the full R2R-CE val-unseen split with GPT-6-Astra, surpassing the previously reported best by 4.13%. Evaluations on RxR-CE, NavRAG-CE, and a real humanoid robot further demonstrate its generalizability.

title: Efficient Natural Language to Temporal Logic Translation for Real-Time Physical AI
abstract: Robots can be controlled to perform tasks with guaranteed correctness when the task instructions are stated in a formal language. Large language models (LLMs) have been widely used to allow users to provide such instructions in natural language (NL), by translating NL into formal language. When deploying such translators on a robot, however, we face limited computing and energy resources, while offloading computation or data to the cloud may be infeasible or undesirable. Yet an LLM is a general-purpose text generator, whereas a formula in a fixed formal language fragment follows a well-defined syntax. We therefore ask whether text generation is needed at all. For the formal language of linear temporal logic (LTL), we show that this translation can instead be broken down into answering a set of questions with pre-defined answers. We then construct a System-One model, a recent class of NL-based classifier, to provide such answers and enable us to translate a natural language instruction into an LTL instruction. On three benchmarks, our translator matches or exceeds the accuracy of the best local LLMs available, at up to one order of magnitude lower runtime and energy consumption. We show that it generalizes to unseen atomic propositions and temporal patterns.

title: A Stationarity-Based Regret Framework for Time-Varying Nonconvex Composite Optimization
abstract: This paper studies time-varying nonconvex composite optimization, where decisions are made sequentially and classical value-based regret notions are generally ill-posed. We introduce a stationarity-based performance framework defined through local regret measures built from first-order optimality conditions, and identify minimal structural requirements under which such measures constitute sound performance criteria. This abstraction encompasses canonical optimality measures, including the proximal-gradient residual, and collapses to classical dynamic regret in convex settings. We then focus on the proximal-gradient residual as a concrete and algorithmically meaningful instantiation for general composite problems. In convex problems, we show that the resulting local regret is equivalent to standard dynamic regret. In nonconvex settings, we establish that sublinear stationarity-based regret is unattainable without temporal regularity, and introduce a gradient-variation budget that captures this necessity. Under this model, we analyze online proximal-gradient methods and prove sublinear regret guarantees in both nested multi-call and fully incremental single-call oracle regimes, highlighting the tradeoff between per-round computational effort and achievable performance. Finally, we demonstrate how the proposed framework extends to nonconvex multiplayer games by interpreting equilibrium-seeking dynamics through stationarity-based regret, and corroborate the theoretical findings with numerical experiments.

title: Actions Speak Louder than Words: Stateful Privacy Sniffing of LLM Agents via Behavioral Covert Channels in Web Interactions
abstract: LLM agents increasingly rely on Web interaction, issuing searches, following links, and reading pages, to complete complex user tasks. Since each action is driven by the agent's private context, including the user's prompt, dialogue history, memory, and connected data, it also opens a new privacy exposure surface. Prior attacks either passively analyze network traffic, which yields only coarse correlations, or hijack the agent through indirect prompt injection, which must place sensitive content in an outgoing field and is blocked by content-level defenses. Whether an attacker can actively recover fine-grained private context without any explicit transmission thus remains insufficiently understood. Our insight is that an agent's benign Web decisions themselves leak private context, as what it chooses to visit encodes whether, which, and in what order it acts, forming a behavioral covert channel. Building on this, we design SNOOP, a stateful hierarchical probing framework that narrows a coarse-to-fine hypothesis tree per task and reconstructs user queries and profiles from the agent's observable paths. Across four agents and three LLM backbones on 500 StackExchange queries and 378 multi-turn iKAT dialogues, SNOOP recovers query concepts with an average F1 of 0.89 and user profiles with an F1 of 0.80, while four representative agent defenses change its recovery by less than 0.03 F1. Since no sensitive content is ever transmitted, content-level inspection cannot detect this leakage; we therefore propose Selection-Obfuscated Retrieval (SOR), which acquires resources under a fixed budget independent of private context and confines the agent's selection to a local snapshot, cutting SNOOP's F1 to 0.39 without additional LLM inference.

title: Learning a Food World Model That Predicts the Next State from Production Data
abstract: Food assembly robots pick ingredients from a pan, and every pick must deliver a target weight. We learn a world model of food picking from 61,773 production picks, labeled automatically by a camera and a scale (self-supervised learning). From the pre-pick heightmap of the pan on a 2.5 mm grid, the commanded pick action, the food and the utensil, the model predicts the post-pick heightmap and the picked mass with uncertainty. We evaluate the mass prediction on 12,294 held-out picks of nine foods. The production controller keeps each pick near its commanded target. The model's root-mean-square error (RMSE) of 10.93 g is 9% lower than that of the commanded target or of a per-food mean. This RMSE is 24% lower than that of the controller's internal mass estimate. Gradient-boosted trees on 20 hand-crafted features have a 0.2 g lower RMSE, but they predict only the mass, not the next state that planning and policy learning need. Using the predicted uncertainty, we decline the most uncertain picks and answer 89.4% of picks with an RMSE of 10.28 g. The prediction barely responds to the commanded volume and depth, because they vary little in closed-loop production. The model also fails without warning at target weights not seen in training. Future directions include action-primitive conditioning and a more general model across foods and utensils. We give recommendations for learning world models from production data.

title: Don't Test Where You Trained: Geographic Overlap Inflates End-to-End Driving Scores
abstract: In NAVSIMv1, the standard benchmark for end-to-end driving, $89.6\%$ of the test scenes lie within 4m of a training scene. We show that this geographic overlap inflates the reported scores. We propose a geographically disjoint split of NAVSIMv1 and an evaluation that compares models trained on either split on the same scenes, which neither has seen in training. All sensor-based models we test, DiffusionDrive, Latent TransFuser, and DrivoR, lose 3.4 to 6.1 PDMS points on these scenes, mainly by leaving the road and coming close to other objects, against 1.5 points for a baseline without sensors. The loss concentrates where a training drive of the original split passed the same place. At all other places, models trained on the original split are no better than those trained on the geographic split. Models trained on the original split predict road geometry that no camera can see. The gap persists when the auxiliary map loss is removed, so the models memorize locations even without being supervised to. On nuScenes, the geographic split cuts SparseDrive's mapping accuracy by $59\%$ and also degrades its planning. Driving scores on logged scenes thus partly measure how well a model remembers the test locations. We release the split to evaluate generalization to new places.

title: QuASAR: Toward an LLM-Assisted Framework for Screening, Prototyping, and Assessing Quantum-Advantage Opportunities in Scientific Computing
abstract: Identifying scientific computations that could benefit from quantum algorithms requires both domain knowledge and fluency in quantum algorithm design, expertise that rarely resides in one person. We report results from QuASAR, an experimental, two-agent, LLM-driven pipeline intended to bridge this gap. One agent screens scientific literature for computational kernels with a plausible quantum-algorithmic analogue and proposes candidates, each backed by citations. A second agent independently verifies those citations. For candidates that survive verification, it reconstructs the source's computational structure, formulates a quantum mapping, builds and executes a prototype, and benchmarks it against classical baselines. We applied this pipeline to ten candidate computations drawn from the astrophysics literature. Nine candidates were carried through to a small-scale, benchmarked prototype. We report three in detail, chosen as the clearest examples with the least redundancy across the set. They span combinatorial optimization, stochastic simulation, and Bayesian inference. The pipeline attempted to supply quantum-design expertise a domain scientist might lack, reconstructing source algorithms where one existed and building original, disclosed mappings where none did. None of the three case studies achieved quantum advantage at the tested scales, and their astrophysical framing has not yet undergone expert validation. What the experiment does show is that the pipeline can turn a published idea into a runnable prototype, which a scientist can then inspect, test against classical methods, and decide whether to pursue. QuASAR is an exploratory framework, offered to the community for evaluation, critique, and further development, with an approach that could broaden the use of quantum computing in scientific research and extend to computational improvements more generally.

title: Verifying and Strengthening Neural Tangent Kernel Theory
abstract: Writing Neural tangent kernel (NTK) theory explains why very wide neural networks trained by gradient methods converge in the lazy-training regime. Its standard proof combines matrix concentration, random Gram matrices, continuous-time dynamics, spectral perturbation, and a bootstrap argument, but has lacked machine-checked verification. We present a Lean\~4 formalisation for two-layer networks, proving an end-to-end theorem: for a smooth bounded activation (instantiated with $σ=\tanh$), frozen biases, paired $\pm 1$ initialisation, and explicit width conditions, gradient flow exists uniquely with probability at least $1-δ$, and $$ \|r(t)\|^2 \leq \|y\|^2 e^{-λ_0 t/2}. $$ The sole data assumption is population NTK non-degeneracy, $λ_0>0$. Initial coercivity, kernel drift, the movement bootstrap, the residual ODE, and flow existence and uniqueness are formally proved. The formalisation also sharpens the standard analysis in two ways. First, replacing the conventional matrix-Bernstein variance proxy with the classical row-covariance proxy yields estimated concentration-width certificates for $\tanh$ that are $36$--$53\times$ smaller at $(m,d)=(16,8)$ and $94$--$121\times$ smaller at $(32,16)$. Lean certifies the inequality; the ratios are numerical. Second, the network Hessian has operator norm $Θ(\sqrt{p})$ on the sup-norm parameter ball (a paper calculation), preventing the expected $O(1/\sqrt{p})$ linearisation bound via sup-norm Taylor estimates. An $L^2$ parameter geometry resolves this issue. Required widths remain polynomial but far beyond practical scales, limiting applicability.

title: Selection Policies for Equal-Byte Mixed-Precision Quantization of Small Language Models
abstract: Can changing which matrices receive 2, 4, or 8 bits improve a small language model without increasing its parameter storage? I compare two parent-selection rules in the same genetic algorithm: a binary-tournament variant and an Alternis-inspired rule. A separate baseline samples repaired random allocations without crossover or mutation. All three use the same MLX affine quantizer, byte ceiling, initialization and candidate allowance within each study. An exploratory study on Qwen3.5-2B evaluates 90 allocations per run. The main study on Qwen3-1.7B evaluates 500 distinct allocations per run over 10 paired seeds. Against uniform four-bit, tournament reduces held-out next-token negative log-likelihood (NLL) by 0.0616 on AG News and 0.0152 on IMDb on average, improving all 10 seeds on each corpus at identical parameter storage. Alternis improves five seeds and ties five on AG News; on IMDb its mean gain is near zero. Random returns uniform four-bit in every seed. The tournament representative answers 156 of 400 ARC-Challenge questions correctly versus 163 for uniform; no accuracy gain is demonstrated on this subset. The result favors this tournament variant for text prediction under the tested protocol, not for compression ratio or task accuracy.

title: Enhancing Attention with Higher-Order Attention
abstract: Current decoder large language models rely on a combination of attention, feed forward and residual layers. The attention used is autoregressive (AR) though this is not strictly correct, as we note. That motivates the introduction of other attention methods that, while also not strictly AR, do enhance the AR character. One is based on a decomposition of mutual information (MI) into a set of Conditional MIs (CMIs) that correlate key tokens with pairs of query tokens. A second, higher-order attention, introduces correlations between contiguous key and query tokens. A third introduces correlations between a set of key and query tokens and uses a Generalized Maximum Entropy Principle to obtain an attention expression spanning a sequence of tokens. All these methods may enhance the information content of the autoregressive probabilities that are used in inference/generation. Applications to contrastive decoding and a systematic analysis of autoregressive probabilities are presented.

title: Practical insights into controlling exponential concentration in quantum machine learning
abstract: Quantum Machine Learning (QML) models are often limited by exponential concentration, where quantum observables become insensitive to input variations as system size increases. In this work, we provide a comparative empirical study of this phenomenon across Fidelity Quantum Kernels (FQK), Projected Quantum Kernels (PQK), and Quantum Extreme Learning (QEL), within a unified observable-based framework based on expectation-value variance. We investigate how measurement locality, entanglement, and circuit expressivity shape concentration across different architectures. Global fidelity-based kernels exhibit strong concentration driven by Hilbert space dimensionality, whereas local-observable approaches reduce but do not eliminate this effect. In PQK and QEL, concentration is primarily governed by entanglement and quantum dynamical expressivity, with reservoir depth emerging as a key factor in QEL architectures. We further study bandwidth scaling as a general mechanism for controlling encoding expressivity across all models. Our results indicate that bandwidth scaling effectively reduces concentration in moderate regimes by restricting the effective expressivity of the encoding, though this protective effect diminishes in highly expressive structural settings.

title: CoPyro: Feeding Copy Proposals to Parallel Drafters
abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates language generation by letting a target model verify several draft tokens in one forward pass. Earlier neural drafters such as EAGLE extend each candidate sequence one token at a time. Recent work has turned to parallel drafters such as DFlash, which predict a whole block at once. Another approach uses n-gram retrieval to find an earlier occurrence of the current context suffix and copy the tokens that followed it directly into the draft. We introduce CoPyro, which feeds these copied tokens into a parallel drafter in place of masks. The drafter learns from context which tokens to keep and which to revise as it predicts the block in its usual forward pass. Across eight benchmarks on Qwen3-4B, CoPyro improves overall acceptance length for all four parallel drafters tested, with gains of 2.19-5.08% when trained on 100K samples. With DFlash trained on 710K samples, overall gains range from 1.08% to 2.00% across the tested model sizes and temperatures. Code generation benefits most in both settings. On Qwen3-8B, processing the proposals adds an average of 0.24 ms per decoding round in Transformers.

title: Hypergraph Structural Entropy-Enhanced Hierarchy-Aware Semi-Supervised Graph Classification
abstract: Semi-supervised graph classification aims to learn graph-level representations by leveraging a large number of unlabeled graphs alongside a small set of labeled ones, effectively mitigating the issue of label scarcity. Despite significant progress by various semi-supervised learning strategies, complex relationships among graph vertices beyond pairwise edges, especially hierarchical structures, remain underexplored by existing methods. In this work, we propose a Hypergraph Structural Entropy-Enhanced hierarchy-aware framework, namely HypSEE, for semi-supervised graph classification. Specifically, we first construct walk-induced and embedding-derived hypergraphs to capture hierarchy-aware local and long-range higher-order relationships within graphs. Then, we devise a hierarchical hypergraph pooling approach guided by hypergraph structural entropy (HSE) to facilitate hierarchical representation learning in hypergraphs. Lastly, we employ an anchor graph-based consistency strategy to mutually align the representations from these two hypergraph views, enhancing the learning efficacy on unlabeled data. Extensive experiments on 8 benchmark datasets demonstrate the state-of-the-art performance of our approach.

title: INSEP: Refusal-Direction Inseparability as a Defense Against Abliteration
abstract: Abliteration is a widely used white-box attack against the safety alignment of large language models (LLMs). It elicits harmful behavior by estimating a refusal direction in the model's activation space and projecting that direction out of the residual-stream write-out matrices. We propose INSEP, a defense that fine-tunes the model to reduce the separability of harmful and benign activations along the refusal direction. Abliteration estimates this direction as a difference in class means and projects it out. Reducing separability weakens the signal the attack relies on. An adversarial eigendecomposition selects the most separable prompt subsets. A low-rank adapter reduces their separation along that direction. Behavioral losses preserve the base model's refusal and the quality of its benign responses during training. We benchmark INSEP against six published defenses under five attacks, across eight LLMs from 1B to 14B parameters and several model families. Beyond response harm, we measure coherence, directness, over-refusal, and MMLU, to distinguish robust refusal from low harm produced by evasive or degraded responses. INSEP ranks first on the mean composite score across all eight base models while retaining utility, in the largest abliteration-defense evaluation reported to date.

title: torchtsetlin: Fast, Interpretable Tsetlin Machines for PyTorch
abstract: The Tsetlin machine learns propositional rules with teams of Tsetlin automata that are driven by reward and penalty rather than gradients, so its models are interpretable by construction and cheap to evaluate. Its software, however, consists of C and CUDA kernels behind scikit-learn-style wrappers that sit outside the deep learning ecosystem. torchtsetlin implements the Tsetlin machine family as ordinary PyTorch modules: vanilla and weighted, coalesced, regression, convolutional over sequences, images and volumes, and dense per-pixel segmentation. The automata are a tensor buffer, so a model moves with .to(device), is saved with state_dict() and learns from a mini-batch with one update(x,y) call. Its core technique is a batched formulation of Type I and Type II feedback, in which automaton transitions become event counts realised as binomial draws, with one commit per mini-batch. On ten benchmarks taken from the existing libraries, it matches their accuracy, and on all but the two smallest it trains 2.4-10.9X faster than PyTsetlinMachineCUDA and 10.3-81.2X faster than tmu on the same GPU. The package is pure Python, MIT-licensed and on PyPI; every number in this paper is reproduced by one script. Code: https://github.com/vlbthambawita/torchtsetlin; package: https://pypi.org/project/torchtsetlin/.

title: From Manufacturing Event Logs to Simulation: Enabling SMEs with Agentic AI for SimPy Simulation Generation
abstract: High expertise and cost barriers exclude small and medium-sized enterprises from discrete-event simulation (DES). We introduce GenAI4SimPy, a multi-agent framework powered by Qwen 3.6 (27B), an open-weight large language model, that automates end-to-end DES generation from manufacturing event logs to executable SimPy models through tool-augmented reasoning and human-in-the-loop validation. Evaluated on three execution blocks from a public smart factory dataset, the framework achieved a mean absolute percentage error of 7.9\% and coverage of failure rate for all three blocks and of throughput for two of three. A fidelity paradox was observed: accurate process-level parameters did not ensure system-level behavioral fidelity, with flow-time and throughput errors driven by misinterpreted observation-window truncation and absent system-level calibration. These results demonstrate that local open-weight models can perform DES generation at accuracy comparable to cloud-based alternatives, while identifying parameter extraction as necessary but insufficient for behavioral validity. Source code and results are available at https://github.com/RaikoPipe/genai4simpy

title: Correct Precedents Induce Policy Violations in On-Device LLM Agents
abstract: Local-cloud agent systems pair a cloud model with a small on-device agent that acts on private data, often as the last check before an irreversible action. We identify, for the first time, a failure in which such an agent is led into a violation by its own correct decisions within a session. After it correctly releases an item whose restriction was lifted, it becomes more likely to release the next item that is still restricted. Because the trigger is a correct decision, a history with no faulty step can still end in a violation. We call this failure correct-precedent generalization and find it in 13 open-weight models from nine developers. A single correct precedent can cut the safe rate of the most affected agent roughly in half, and the risk compounds when a refused request is simply sent again in a new session. Interventions on the agent's history indicate that it carries its decision on the released item over to the restricted one instead of checking that item's status. Building on this finding, we propose Paired Decision Distillation (PDD), which distills the decisions of a weakly affected teacher into a LoRA adapter. PDD restores the safe rate to nearly 100% in every distilled model, without extra prompt text or model calls.

title: Disentangling Verbalized Evaluation Awareness and Refusal through Neuron-Level Intervention
abstract: As large reasoning models (LRMs) become more capable, reliable evaluation becomes essential. LRMs can sometimes recognize that they are being evaluated, a phenomenon known as \emph{evaluation awareness}. This phenomenon raises concerns about whether safety behavior, particularly refusal behavior, generalizes from evaluation to deployment. Prior work manipulates \emph{verbalized evaluation awareness (VEA)} through activation steering and observes higher refusal rates when VEA is present, but the mechanisms underlying this connection remain poorly understood. We identify \emph{VEA neurons} by contrasting their activations in VEA and non-VEA reasoning segments. Intervening on 5,000 VEA neurons reduces the VEA rate from 12.6--51.8\% to at most 1.4\% across the model benchmark combinations in our main experiments, and lowers a probe score for unverbalized evaluation awareness (unVEA). In QwQ-32B, VEA-neuron intervention also reduces refusal even in rollouts without VEA; VEA text itself explains only 4--10\% of the decrease. We further show that their down-projection vectors contain refusal components, and preserving these components during intervention partially restores refusal while maintaining VEA suppression, accounting for about half of the refusal decrease and providing a mechanistic explanation for the connection between evaluation awareness and refusal. Finally, across the OLMo 3 SFT, DPO, and RLVR checkpoints, the VEA rate on SorryBench and StrongREJECT is similar after SFT and DPO but substantially higher after RLVR, alongside an increase in the number of VEA neurons. Together, these findings show that VEA text itself has a limited effect on refusal, and that VEA neurons integrate evaluation awarenss and refusal.

title: An LLM-Assisted Multi-Objective AutoML Framework for Efficient Network Intrusion Detection
abstract: Conventional Machine Learning (ML)-based Intrusion Detection Systems (IDSs) require manual design, optimize only detection performance, and neglect inference latency and model size, which are critical for resource-constrained Internet of Things (IoT) and Electric Vehicle Charging System (EVCS) deployments. Automated ML (AutoML) reduces manual effort but explores broad search spaces inefficiently. Meanwhile, Multi-Objective Optimization (MOO) methods lack guided search initialization, leading to long search times. This paper proposes a Large Language Model-Assisted Multi-Objective Automated ML (LLM-MOO-AutoML) framework for efficient intrusion detection. A local Llama 3.1 8B model analyzes a compact dataset profile and generates a bounded, validated policy for automated data balancing (AutoDP) and feature engineering (AutoFE). This policy narrows the search space for Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm III (NSGA-III), which jointly optimizes the LightGBM feature-selection threshold and key hyperparameters across three objectives: maximizing weighted F1-score, minimizing 99th-percentile (P99) inference latency ratio, and minimizing model size ratio. Experiments on CICIDS2017, IoTID20, and CICEVSE2024 demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves the highest weighted F1-scores on CICIDS2017 (99.788%), IoTID20 (99.778%), and CICEVSE2024 (99.989%), with feature sets reduced to as few as 10 features, P99 latency as low as 0.00038 ms, and model size as small as 0.1073 MB. The LLM-guided configuration reduced NSGA-III search time relative to unconstrained multi-objective search on all datasets at the largest trial budget and in most comparisons at smaller budgets, indicating that dataset-aware search-space reduction supports efficient, deployment-aware intrusion detection.

title: From Novel Combinations to Informative Absence: Structural permission, communicative opportunity, and form choice in language learning
abstract: Language learners must infer which novel expressions are grammatically licensed and when continued absence is evidence against them. Our generative theory unites these capacities via counterfactual expression opportunities, decomposing utterance generation into structural permission, communicative opportunity, and form choice. First, shared predictive continuations recover structural permission for unseen word-construction pairings across 30 artificial grammars (mean AUC 0.945 after 120 sentences). Second, under hierarchical uncertainty, we derive a joint evidence law linking omissions to context diversity and within-context repetition, and an exact finite-sample context-refinement inequality. Thus, observing related expressions calibrates expected use to sharpen negative evidence, and higher expected use can drive steeper posterior declines for stronger-permission candidates (reversing initial order after six omissions in a fixed-rate example). Third, we prove that while raw counts confound semantic availability and form selection, scene-level opportunity observations identify both. Empirically, reanalyzing adult and child artificial-language experiments shows meaning-conditioned restriction; judgments of restricted combinations improve held-out production predictions across 399 participants (+0.036 nats/production). Naturalistic child-directed and child speech (11 families, six corpora) shows pervasive source-level usage clustering beyond lexical, number, and dependency-role controls, grounding hierarchical rate uncertainty. Finally, modeling causative judgments across five languages shows that structural compatibility and calibrated usage probabilities draw on distinct distributional, semantic, and discriminative cues. Together, these findings show how the organization and calibration of communicative opportunities govern the evidential value of linguistic absence.

title: Cannot Wait to Verify: Parallel Drafting to Eliminate Verifier Idle Time in Speculative Decoding
abstract: Autoregressive inference in large transformer models is limited by token-level sequential execution, resulting in high latency and low GPU utilization. Speculative decoding (SD) mitigates this bottleneck by introducing a draft-and-verifier model. However, the drafting stage remains sequential, leaving the verifier idle and underutilizing compute. To address this, we propose a plug-and-play drafting adaptive drafting method that parallelizes inference across transformer layers during draft generation. Starting from a shared hidden state, our approach evaluates multiple layers in parallel and verifies consistency by measuring divergence in hidden-state space. Layer-wise draft states are accepted when deviations are small; otherwise, a correction step is applied. By exploiting redundancy across transformer layers, our method accelerates draft generation and improves hardware utilization without modifying architectures or requiring retraining. Experimental results on NLP tasks show that our method speeds up the drafting stage by up to $1.65\times$ with minimal degradation in accuracy, while maintaining the same performance as SD.

title: Neural Defend Ranks #1 in Global Audio Deepfake Detection Benchmark - ARCAS on the Podonos Independent Leaderboard
abstract: Commercial detectors of AI-generated audio are usually promoted with results on internal test sets that buyers cannot inspect. Independent benchmarks with private labels give a more reliable comparison. We report the results of Neural Defend's ARCAS foundation models on the Podonos audio deepfake detection benchmark, an independent leaderboard that scores commercial detection APIs and open-source detectors on one held-out set of real speech and speech from current text-to-speech and voice-cloning systems, delivered in six file formats, against labels that only Podonos holds. In the release of 29 October 2026, which covers 28 systems from 16 commercial vendors and the leading open models, ARCAS 290M and the smaller ARCAS 90M share first place, ahead of every other commercial system, including Resemble AI, Hiya, Pindrop, Hive, and Reality Defender. Both models make fewer errors than any other system by a statistically clear margin, keep false positives and false negatives in balance at their default threshold, process every submitted file without rejection, and sit on the accuracy--latency frontier of the leaderboard. As for every commercial system added since Podonos retired its API runner, the ARCAS predictions were submitted by Neural Defend and scored by Podonos against its private labels. We describe the benchmark's construction and protocol in full, reproduce the complete leaderboard and its history across five releases, and analyse error balance, statistical separation, speed, and the gap between commercial and open-source detectors. The results agree with the companion evaluation of ARCAS 290M on the complete test sets of ten public benchmarks and establish ARCAS as the most accurate AI-generated audio detector evaluated on this independent benchmark.

title: TSIR: Ray-Traced Triangle Splats for Inverse Rendering
abstract: Inverse rendering enables realistic relighting for visual effects and augmented reality. However, overlapping Gaussian primitives complicate surface recovery and require costly multi-layer traversal and compositing for light transport. We propose TSIR, a two-stage inverse rendering method that reconstructs relightable triangle splats from multi-view images. The first stage prepares opaque triangle splats with learnable vertex shading normals. The second stage directly traces these surfaces to estimate materials through Monte Carlo integration of direct illumination and indirect reflections, reducing reliance on multi-layer compositing. Anti-aliasing improves rendering quality while maintaining efficiency. Experiments demonstrate higher relighting quality than the evaluated baselines and more efficient anti-aliasing than supersampling.

We propose TSIR, a two-stage inverse rendering method that reconstructs relightable triangle splats from multi-view images. The first stage prepares opaque triangle splats with learnable vertex shading normals. The second stage directly traces these surfaces to estimate materials through Monte Carlo integration of direct illumination and indirect reflections, reducing reliance on multi-layer compositing. Anti-aliasing improves rendering quality while maintaining efficiency. Experiments demonstrate higher relighting quality than the evaluated baselines and more efficient anti-aliasing than supersampling.

title: Benchmarking EEG feature families for ADHD research in children and adolescents: performance and explainability across attention tasks
abstract: Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder varies in presentation. Diagnosis requires clinical and developmental assessment. Reproducible electroencephalography measures may complement clinical and behavioural characterisation, but differing feature definitions and evaluation methods hinder comparison. We compared seven feature families and four combinations across attention tasks and assessed the stability of held-out explanations. Two serious games yielded four overlapping attention-task cohorts of 123-140 participants each. Repeated nested participant-held-out evaluation assessed recruitment-group discrimination. Exploratory paired participant-cluster bootstrap tests corrected for multiplicity in two separate families: 72 individual-task contrasts and 18 fusion contrasts. For eight configurations selected after inspecting predictive results, we explained held-out native probabilities before calibration. In the strongest task context, the highest configuration mean AUROC over three repetitions was 0.773, with a fixed-prediction 95% interval of 0.692-0.854 unadjusted for selecting the maximum. Precision, sensitivity and specificity were 0.740, 0.556 and 0.861. In that task, the paired AUROC difference for connectivity minus spectral features averaged +0.2083 across six classifiers and the common 8 s and 16 s durations, with pointwise 95% CI 0.1076-0.3072 and adjusted p = 0.0036. F4-AF4 beta-band coherence led repetition-level attribution summaries in five selected procedures and was selected in every fit. Other contexts showed weaker discrimination and less consistent retention of leading scientific inputs. No general classifier winner emerged. Connectivity and its recurring coherence input warrant independent replication, but do not justify a universal feature recommendation. These exploratory findings do not establish causal task effects, disease mechanisms or diagnostic validity.

title: DPMA: Learning to Compress Mixture-of-Experts Models
abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures offer high computational efficiency, but storing all experts requires substantial memory and limits deployment on resource-constrained hardware. Most retraining-free MoE compression methods commit to either pruning or merging experts, often with a uniform compression ratio across layers. We introduce DPMA (Differentiable Prune Merge Absorb), which jointly learns compression operations and layer-wise expert allocation through gradient descent under a global expert budget. Separate learnable coefficients allow DPMA to prune experts, merge their parameters, and absorb their routing contributions by forwarding routing weights to retained experts. These coefficients and expert assignments are optimised to match the original model's outputs on calibration data while its weights remain frozen. Across four MoE models, eight multiple-choice benchmarks, and five compression ratios, DPMA achieves the highest accuracy averaged over benchmarks and compression ratios on each model among the evaluated methods. At $75\%$ expert reduction, it outperforms the strongest baseline on every model, with gains of up to $6.7$ percentage points.

title: PathOPEN: A pathologist-curated histopathology dataset for visual question answering
abstract: PathOPEN is a histopathology dataset for visual question answering. Two clinical pathologists selected 157 cases with 229 available original images and wrote open-ended, five-option multiple-choice and close-ended (yes/no) questions. They supplied both a correct and a wrong answer for 201 of the 309 open-ended questions. Each case records the organ, pathology category and regional anatomy, and each image records its magnification. The dataset includes 6,870 augmented images and four manifests that select subsets to improve balance by individual metadata field. Five additional pathologists and two vision-language model judges rated items with scoring rubrics, and six models answered questions zero-shot across the three formats. The metadata support subgroup evaluation, and the paired answers can be used to construct preference examples.

title: EAF-TTS: Rethinking Codec-Latent Coordinates for Flow TTS
abstract: Latent text-to-speech (TTS) systems generate codec latents decoded by a frozen decoder, but good reconstruction does not ensure geometry suitable for Flow generation from isotropic Gaussian noise. We present Embedded Acoustic Flow TTS (EAF-TTS), an acoustic-latent adaptation of ELF with phone- and duration-conditioned generation, shared-network terminal correction, and frozen WaveVAE decoding. EAF-TTS supports a fixed ZCA interface estimated from training data and adding no learned parameters. The codec, conditioning modules, Flow backbone, and 20-call inference are shared. The intervention is the full ZCA coordinate protocol---training and sampling coordinates, induced loss metric, and terminal perturbation---not an inference-only transform. In single-speaker LJSpeech, the 64-D training-latent covariance has condition number 1355.44. On text-disjoint Val399 strict-GT with fixed E100 raw checkpoints across three matched seeds, ZCA improves UTMOS22 Strong---an automatic naturalness proxy, not human MOS---by $+0.405\pm0.027$ over Scalar normalization (mean $\pm$ seed SD of per-seed paired differences). Absolute scores remain below codec-reference levels. Without retraining, ZCA-5 retains $+0.375\pm0.027$ UTMOS over Scalar-20 while reducing generation-path RTF by $3.34\times$. This three-seed analysis shows no statistically detectable WER or exact-match degradation, but does not establish equivalence. ZCA-3 gives $5.03\times$ with a $+0.165$ UTMOS advantage. At matched reduced call counts, ZCA's advantage shrinks, indicating full-step headroom rather than better low-step integration. A secondary text-only selected-checkpoint result is directionally consistent but confounded by checkpoint type. We claim only proxy-naturalness and measured quality--latency effects within this protocol; human listening, blind text, and broader validation remain necessary.

title: Mind World Models: Joint Learning of Motor EEG Representations and Action-Conditioned World Dynamics
abstract: Motor decoding from electroencephalography (EEG) supports non-invasive brain-computer interfaces, yet existing methods either rely on costly cue-based trials and coarse categorical labels or use pretraining objectives that do not directly capture how movement unfolds, limiting their ability to learn transferable motor representations. To this end, we propose the Mind World Model (MWM), a framework that learns motor EEG representations from scalable naturalistic EEG and egocentric video without action annotations. MWM treats EEG observed up to the current frame as the latent action of a world model: a mind model encodes the EEG, and a world model uses it to predict the representation of a future frame, yielding a movement-grounded pretraining objective. We further introduce the Lateralization-Aware Transformer (LAT), which uses frame averaging to separate shared bilateral from side-specific lateral features, encoding hemispheric correspondence to reduce the burden of learning left-right relationships from data. MWM pretraining produces two models: a mind model for downstream motor decoding and a world model that can be adapted to prediction conditioned on real actions, opening a scalable and flexible path to collect egocentric data for embodied AI. Across 9 classification and 7 regression tasks, the mind model improves task-averaged balanced accuracy by 5.9% and Pearson correlation by 16.2% relative to the strongest baseline in each task family. Compared with an inverse-dynamics latent-action baseline, the world model achieves lower prediction error and benefits 3.3 times more from matched real actions within recordings and 4.7 times more on held-out subjects.

title: Non-LLM Continual-Learning AI: From Instrument Readings to a Balloon's Lift
abstract: Tersive White Paper 2. Tersive is a reasoning system that works from a confined body of knowledge and accepts only what it can test. No LLM is used in its reasoning. What it discovered. Tersive was given four instruments with meaningless names and a sealed sample of gas. It was not told what the instruments measured, that a law existed, or that the law fails anywhere. From its own experiments it found the ideal gas law, including its constant. It also found absolute zero by extrapolation, with no limit given: all six runs’ 95% intervals contain −273.15 °C. When the instrument ranges were widened without warning, it refuted its own claim that the law holds everywhere. It then described where the law holds, placing argon’s edge within 0.4 °C of argon’s critical temperature. What it did with it. Tersive kept the law as established knowledge. It then used it, together with standard physics it was given, to predict the lift of a sealed envelope of gas in air, a question it had never seen. Air’s density was never given; Tersive computed it from its own law. Across 630 questions its predictions agreed with CoolProp real-gas references to within 0.29% of the displaced air’s weight. Helium’s lift was within 0.23% in every case, and it predicted that argon sinks. Continual learning. In one investigation Tersive completed a full cycle: it acquired a law by experiment and kept it; it used that law as a premise in a new question; it recognised where its knowledge ran out and reported exactly what was missing; it placed new general facts whose connection to the problem it was not told; it completed the answer, with no change to its reasoning machinery and no loss of earlier abilities. These are internal experiments and have not been peer reviewed. Next steps: replication on data chosen by an outside party, and a test in which a gap in Tersive’s knowledge triggers its own experiments. Continues Tersive White Paper 1 (doi:10.5281/zenodo.24371620).

title: Language Model Harnesses can be Compositional Generalizers
abstract: Modern language models (LMs) are post-trained and deployed as agents inside a "harness", but standard harness designs accumulate context that the neural network is forced to generalize to, making training for long-horizon tasks expensive and time-consuming. We study an alternative emerging path: training inherently neurosymbolic LM harnesses, which externalize and manage context programmatically to compose existing LM capabilities. We hypothesize that training around these harnesses can offer a better return on compute by enabling compositional generalization, as they can learn to decompose complex problems so that every observation their neural LM receives is locally in-distribution, even when the full task is novel. We find that harnesses like the Recursive Language Model (RLM) learn such decompositions readily under reinforcement learning post-training: (1) we demonstrate that training only on short tasks can generalize to tasks 2-64$\times$ longer while the base neural LM improves less, and (2) training on one domain transfers to novel domains that share latent structure. On messier, complex tasks, we find that we can target individual LLM calls within a harness by generating and training on easier, synthetically generated surrogate environments with fake tool / sub-calls, a technique we call surrogate harness training. From this finding, we train RLM-27B on synthetic data, and show it improves Qwen3.8-27B in the same RLM harness on a hard suite of long-context tasks like CTC-Bench and ExpertLongBench by 26.9% on average while using $\sim$2$\times$ fewer tokens at inference time. Finally, we show that harnesses can compose over these newly learned decompositions using recursive sub-harness calls.

title: Ref-YOLO-World: Decoupling Text-Side Computation for Efficient Referring Expression Comprehension on Edge Devices
abstract: Many high-accuracy referring expression comprehension (REC) methods produce image-dependent multimodal representations. These representations must be recomputed for every video frame, even when the referring expression remains unchanged. Fast open-vocabulary detectors such as YOLO-World instead pre-encode text once and reuse it throughout the stream. However, encoding each referring expression as a single embedding prevents explicit token-level correspondence. We propose Ref-YOLO-World, which separates text-side computation that depends only on the referring expression from image processing and reuses its outputs across frames. Two lightweight modules inject cached per-token text features into YOLO-World's detection path. Ref-YOLO-World achieves 81.29% Acc@0.5 on RefCOCOg val, the highest among REC models with a decoupled text branch, and consistently outperforms a fine-tuned YOLO-World. Precomputation reduces per-image inference time by 18.5%, yielding 47.0 FPS. A Core ML version runs at 15.73 FPS on an iPhone 15 Pro, demonstrating efficient on-device REC. Code is available at https://github.com/sakusaku3939/Ref-YOLO-World.

title: ROSWORLD: When Digital Task Competence Meets Physical Execution
abstract: Computer-use agents now solve most desktop tasks through direct software input, but a robot using the same computer must turn GUI knowledge into physical contact with a keyboard and mouse. We introduce ROSWorld, a benchmark that couples a physically simulated robot workstation to a live OSWorld desktop, so that a robot and a desktop agent pursue the same goals under the same official evaluators. The evaluated model receives observations only from the workstation camera views and operates the peripherals through either a single-arm rigid probe or dual-arm dexterous hands. Across five frontier models and 40 tasks in ten applications, models that complete 31-39 tasks on the desktop complete at most 23 with the probe and 28 with the hands. Paired trajectory analysis shows that models adapt their interaction strategies toward keyboard input, yet physical execution frequently fails through missed presses, incorrect targets, and unintended contacts. ROSWorld makes the gap between knowing what to do on a computer and physically doing it measurable.

title: TWICE: Toward a digital twin of ICU patients with a generative event model for forecasting trajectories and simulating treatment response
abstract: A digital twin of a patient in intensive care would forecast the patient's course and what a treatment would change. Generative event models, trained to continue a patient's electronic health record (EHR), have been proposed as a path toward such twins. We trained TWICE, a 79M-parameter decoder-only transformer, on the ICU records of one academic health system (127,332 training patients and 1.57 billion tokens). We evaluated it on clinical prediction tasks, generation fidelity, individual trajectories and counterfactual validation. Reading 19 clinical outcomes off 50 simulated futures, with no task-specific training, TWICE matched the best of 144 supervised configurations on held-out patients (mean AUROC 0.836 vs. 0.834). It led on events that change care within a day and trailed on death. With the training data fixed, more and longer simulated futures were worth more than a 6.8-fold larger model. Its generated records matched real ones closely and were as specific to each patient as its own variability allowed. Its predicted risk rose as events approached. Pre-specified controls showed that it reproduced the side effects of drugs and was barely moved by an inert drug. On the values that treatments are given to correct, however, an opposite treatment moved its forecasts like the right one. TWICE forecasts ICU events about as well as task-specific models, and we see it as a step toward a digital twin of the ICU patient.

title: GERF: A Token-Efficient Multimodal Retrieval Framework for Schema-Guided Scientific Information Extraction
abstract: Scientific information extraction (IE) is a fundamental component of AI for Science, transforming experimental knowledge embedded in scientific literature into structured and traceable data for evidence synthesis, scientific database construction, and data-driven discovery. However, critical experimental details are often distributed across text, tables, figures, captions, and surrounding discussion, making them difficult to recover using conventional text-only extraction. Existing LLM-based and multimodal RAG pipelines typically rely on full-document context or coarse page-level retrieval, introducing substantial irrelevant evidence and high textual and visual token costs. We propose GERF, a Graph-based Evidence Retrieval Framework for token-efficient, schema-guided multimodal scientific IE. GERF represents each article as a heterogeneous evidence graph that connects schema fields, text chunks, figures, and figure-derived content through semantic and structural relations. Using schema fields as retrieval anchors, GERF combines direct semantic retrieval, Random Walk with Restart, and null-aware evidence expansion to construct compact, field-specific multimodal evidence packages. Visual interpretation is applied only to graph-selected figures, avoiding indiscriminate processing of the entire document. We evaluate GERF from two complementary perspectives: evidence retrieval quality and pipeline-level input-token consumption. On the expert-annotated SOFC-Exp corpus, GERF retrieves gold-supported evidence for 94.55% of the evaluated field instances, providing broad field-level evidence coverage for downstream extraction. In the token comparison, GERF reduces average input-token usage by 73.40% relative to full-context processing and uses fewer tokens than the evaluated page-level pipelines.

GERF represents each article as a heterogeneous evidence graph that connects schema fields, text chunks, figures, and figure-derived content through semantic and structural relations. Using schema fields as retrieval anchors, GERF combines direct semantic retrieval, Random Walk with Restart, and null-aware evidence expansion to construct compact, field-specific multimodal evidence packages. Visual interpretation is applied only to graph-selected figures, avoiding indiscriminate processing of the entire document. We evaluate GERF from two complementary perspectives: evidence retrieval quality and pipeline-level input-token consumption. On the expert-annotated SOFC-Exp corpus, GERF retrieves gold-supported evidence for 94.55% of the evaluated field instances, providing broad field-level evidence coverage for downstream extraction. In the token comparison, GERF reduces average input-token usage by 73.40% relative to full-context processing and uses fewer tokens than the evaluated page-level pipelines.

title: An Asymptotic One-Sample Surrogate for Non-Gaussian ERM with General Convex Regularization
abstract: We study convex empirical risk minimization (ERM) with non-Gaussian features and nonsmooth penalties through a surrogate driven by a single Gaussian vector. The surrogate preserves the penalty and calibrates its coefficients using the actual joint law of the feature-label model. We prove that this population calibration exists and is unique. We prove a Gaussian approximation for fresh prediction scores when the data satisfy a Poincaré inequality. Together with regularity conditions on the losses, this approximation yields agreement between the ERM minimizer and its surrogate in normalized means and prediction variances, as well as formulas for prediction and classification risks. The result covers general uniformly strongly convex penalties and pure Lasso under projection anti-concentration. The core proof relies on a cavity Hamilton-Jacobi argument that compares the main statistics of the two minimizers without differentiating the penalty.

title: Cecilia: Towards Layout-Inclusive Optical Music Recognition
abstract: Reconstructing an editable music score requires musical events, sung text and the instructions that organise them on the page. Existing recognition targets often omit part of this information, while direct MusicXML prediction repeats substantial structural markup. We introduce Cecilia, a compact representation of canonicalised MusicXML that retains musical content, lyric attachments and layout instructions. Cecilia-OMR predicts this representation through metadata and measure-bounded music segments from shared visual memory. A learned count head determines the number of output segments. Across paired complete scores under a common tokeniser, the ratio of mean MusicXML to Cecilia sequence lengths is 27.73. Cecilia-OMR outperforms Legato 2 on Camera String Quartets and both Lieder conditions, with a four-condition OpenScore macro normalised edit distance of 0.2232 against 0.2998. Separate evaluations of lyrics, notation trees and rendered layout reveal complementary aspects of reconstruction and quantify the contribution of layout instructions. Training-stage, reward and candidate-selection studies further examine how recognition changes across model adaptation and decoding.

title: Dem2TA: Beyond Pixels, Towards Perception
abstract: Task-oriented image signal processors (ISPs) adapt RAW-to-RGB processing for downstream perception. However, explicit demosaicing is often simplified, kept fixed, or optimized primarily for reconstruction quality, leaving this stage insufficiently integrated into task adaptation. We propose \textbf{Dem2TA}, a framework that incorporates fidelity-supervised demosaicing into the adaptation of the perception pipeline. Starting from a pretrained demosaicing model, we jointly adapt the reconstruction frontend and downstream network using reconstruction and task supervision, together with complementary semantic and task representation alignment. We then freeze the adapted frontend and jointly optimize a lightweight local ISP with the downstream model to refine task-specific rendering without changing the reconstructed linear RGB. Experiments on synthetic RAW detection and box-prompted segmentation demonstrate the effectiveness of representation-guided joint adaptation and subsequent local rendering. Evaluation on a manually verified real-capture dataset further supports transfer beyond synthetic inputs. Compared with TA-ISP on the same adapted foundation, Dem2TA improves detection AP by 0.46 points and segmentation IoU by 1.06 points on synthetic COCO RAW, and segmentation IoU by 0.63 points on real captures.

title: ReactDrive: Self-Reactive Driving World Model
abstract: The world evolves through the dynamics of its constituent entities and their interactions, with changes in one entity influencing the behavior of others. To simulate this evolution under different actions, interactive world models need to capture the resulting agent responses as part of the world's own dynamics. In autonomous driving, errors in modeling these responses can misrepresent maneuver safety and undermine the reliability of generated videos used for policy evaluation and learning. To formalize this intrinsic requirement for driving world model, we define self-reactivity as the capability to model agent responses from observed history and a specified ego action, and generate visual futures that reflect those responses without prescribed future agent trajectories. To realize this capability, we introduce ReactDrive, a driving world model that jointly learns agent dynamics and visual generation through a shared agent state representation. Within this framework, dynamics supervision grounds a reactive dynamics prior in observed agent states, while the video objective jointly optimizes the self-reactivity and visual realism. Experiments show improved agent responses, ego controllability, and video quality, a 96.0% preference for agent reactivity in human comparisons across five baselines, and better downstream planning through augmentation with generated videos. We hope this work encourages the community to recognize self-reactivityas a foundational capability for developing and evaluating interactive world models. Project page: https://reactdrive.github.io/ .

title: Forecasts that change the future: a closed timelike curve model on quantum hardware
abstract: Published forecasts can bring about the outcomes they announce or provoke responses that avert them. We ask which forecasts remain consistent once people act on them, by conditioning forecasts on agreement with the outcomes they induce. Under a uniform forecast prior, each retained forecast is weighted by its probability of coming true. This rule can be implemented by quantum postselection in a closed timelike curve model built from quantum teleportation. Deutsch's stationary rule gives different weights. In a stylised recession model with a strongly self-defeating response, the recession forecast receives weight 0.0001 under agreement conditioning and 0.30 under the stationary rule. Under a uniform prior the two rules coincide when the outcome ignores the forecast. The rule is classically computable, so the hardware experiment tests how faithfully a processor implements it and gives no computational advantage. Its plan was published before two confirmatory sessions, which ran on IBM Kingston on consecutive days. After readout mitigation the plan's tests of leakage, acceptance and equivalence to a classical filter were met, and a separate witness certified entanglement in the primary circuits. Where the response always averts a forecast recession, the forecast that should be excluded retained weight 0.011 with one two-qubit gate, 0.027 (95% interval 0.015 to 0.039) with two to three and 0.062 with five to seven. Without readout mitigation the second figure is 0.070, above the limit of 0.05. A classically correlated pair in place of the entangled pair gave 0.021.

title: MRI-Driven Dual-Energy CT Synthesis via Conditional Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models for MRI-only Radiotherapy and Protontherapy
abstract: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) provides excellent soft-tissue contrast without ionizing radiation but lacks the electron-density information needed for radiotherapy dose calculation. Dual-energy computed tomography (DECT) improves tissue characterization and stopping-power ratio (SPR) estimation for proton therapy, but requires additional radiation exposure. We developed a denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) to synthesize high- and low-energy CT (sHECT and sLECT) simultaneously from a single MRI scan. Retrospective paired MRI-DECT data from patients receiving head-and-neck proton therapy were used to train and evaluate a multi-decoder DDPM with SwinViT or ResUNet denoisers. Performance was compared with Pix2PixGAN and CycleGAN using image-quality metrics, Hounsfield unit (HU) errors, anatomical profiles, and SPR maps and uncertainties. The DDPM outperformed both generative adversarial network baselines in visual fidelity and quantitative image quality. For sHECT and sLECT, respectively, mean absolute errors were 36.29 +/- 5.25 and 43.72 +/- 6.77 HU; peak signal-to-noise ratios were 27.44 +/- 1.06 and 26.26 +/- 0.98 dB; structural similarity indices were 0.89 +/- 0.02 and 0.87 +/- 0.03; and normalized cross-correlations were 0.95 +/- 0.01 and 0.94 +/- 0.01. The synthesized images preserved anatomical boundaries, while uncertainties in derived SPR maps remained within the expected acceptable range. MRI-based DECT synthesis using DDPM may provide tissue-specific information for proton therapy planning while reducing the need for radiation-based DECT acquisition.

title: SUPERVISE: A Unified Framework for Standardized and Reproducible Superpixel Evaluation
abstract: Image segmentation into superpixels is a widely used technique in computer vision, with a large body of work developed over the years. Yet, its evaluation remains poorly standardized, as methods are compared under heterogeneous protocols, across inconsistent scale ranges, and with redundant or misaligned metric subsets. In this work, we introduce SUPERVISE (SUperpixel PERformance VISualization and Evaluation), a unified and reproducible benchmark that addresses these longstanding inconsistencies. Built on a scale-normalized protocol based on interpolation over the actual number of generated superpixels, SUPERVISE enables fair and consistent cross-method comparisons. We leverage this standardized framework to conduct the first large-scale statistical analysis of 20 evaluation metrics across 7 datasets and 31 methods, revealing strong inter-metric correlations and significant redundancy that challenge common evaluation practices. These findings provide empirical support for reporting a compact set of representative metrics. SUPERVISE is released as a lightweight, modular framework built on precomputed shared label maps, making large-scale reproducible evaluation accessible to the community. All code, label maps, and evaluation results are publicly available at: https://github.com/waldo-j/supervise

title: Supervaluationism about vagueness and indeterminacy: A judgment-aggregation perspective
abstract: Supervaluationism about vagueness and indeterminacy is based on the idea that some sentences, or predicates within them, have multiple competing interpretations or specifications. A sentence is deemed determinately true if and only if it is true according to all specifications; and determinately false if and only if it is false according to all specifications. In all other cases, the sentence is assigned no determinate truth-value. Supervaluationism, however, is only one way of taking into account the verdicts of different specifications -- in technical terms, "aggregating" those verdicts. In this paper, we introduce insights from the theory of judgment aggregation to study a broad class of different aggregation functions. This allows us to offer an axiomatic characterization of supervaluationism, which, in turn, locates it precisely within a larger logical space of possible approaches to vagueness and indeterminacy. Among other results, we axiomatically compare supervaluationism with subvaluationism, the epistemic theory of vagueness, and Strong Kleene and LP logics.

title: Parameter-Efficient Adaptation of Qwen3-VL for Handwritten Mathematical Expression Recognition
abstract: Handwritten mathematical expression recognition (HMER) requires joint recovery of symbol identity and two-dimensional syntax, so a locally plausible transcription may still be structurally wrong. We study whether a compact vision-language model can be adapted to generate linearized Symbol Label Graphs (SLGs) under limited computing resources. Starting from a 4-bit Qwen3-VL-4B checkpoint, we apply rank-16 Low-Rank Adaptation to the vision, language, attention, and MLP modules and train with instruction-formatted CROHME 2019 examples. We compare this model with an internally implemented ViT-Transformer baseline, a zero-shot Qwen3-VL configuration, and additional internally evaluated alternatives. On the 1,198 valid CROHME test examples, the CROHME-only model obtains 524 exact matches (43.74%) and a corpus BLEU-4 score of 77.67, compared with 4.92% and 43.26 for the task-specific ViT baseline. An ablation that adds 2,000 manually written, formula-guided samples decreases exact match to 42.32%, exposing a domain-alignment issue rather than an automatic benefit from more data. The principal contribution is therefore an evidence-backed, resource-efficient formulation of HMER as multimodal structural generation, together with a controlled data-composition ablation and an analysis of the remaining gap between local token overlap and globally correct structure.

title: Integral Multipliers and Arithmetic Obstructions for Two-Hidden-Layer ReLU Maxima
abstract: We study exact representations of maximum functions by ReLU networks with two hidden layers and integer parameters. The least positive output multiplier is two for the six-input maximum, and either two or six for the seven-input maximum. We obtain these bounds from integral cubical fillings and a coefficient-preserving passage from polytope identities to networks. For the coordinate-facet complex of the six-simplex, we compute a coning index of six over the integers and three after inverting two, allowing arbitrary integral directions within each facet. A class in the homology of the unrestricted kernel complex characterizes the remaining seven-input problem; its vanishing is equivalent to an integral filling of a fixed target. We also construct a finite character that separates rational from three-local representability in a dictionary containing two known constructions and all pairs of edge-disjoint three-edge forests. This obstruction permits nonsymmetric coefficients and is confined to the specified dictionary. Control of lower-dimensional remainders yields a sufficient criterion in the top-dimensional quotient. Exact certificates and verification programs accompany the finite calculations.

title: Feedback-Driven Prompt Refinement for Educational AI: Affective Trajectory Estimation and Bloom's Taxonomy Classification
abstract: Contribution: This study has shown that a shared prompt-refinement procedure, guided by distinct affective and cognitive feedback signals, can improve held-out reference agreement and multi-label classification while reducing affective-generation variability without executor parameter updates. Background: Industry 4.0 has increased demand for personalized technical education across interconnected computing and engineering domains, while prompt sensitivity and generation variability have complicated dependable interpretation of instructional dialogue and learning outcomes. Research Questions: The study has examined whether task-specific feedback can improve affective-reference agreement, generation consistency, and cognitive classification without updating executor parameters. Methodology: A secondary language model has revised executor prompts using executor-output discrepancies against model-generated affective references for four dialogues and annotated Bloom labels for 70 learning outcomes; separate sets of 100 EduTalk conversations and 1,000 outcomes have supported held-out comparisons. Small refinement sets, unvalidated affective references, and absent learner-outcome measures have constrained interpretation. Findings: Affective mean absolute error has decreased from 0.742 to 0.702 and mean generation standard deviation from 0.307 to 0.238, while Bloom micro-F1 has increased from 0.687 to 0.893 and exact-match subset accuracy from 0.418 to 0.636. These findings have supported prompt refinement as a candidate approach for developing adaptive technical instruction, while its effects on workforce learning remain to be established.

title: Budgeted Subset Selection with a Transferable Learned Value Model
abstract: Subset selection is a fundamental task in machine learning, statistics and combinatorial optimisation, with applications in active learning, band selection, input selection and experimental design. The utility of a subset depends on information revealed only after the selection, such as labels or responses, and on interactions among selected candidates. Existing approaches combine value estimation and redundancy control in application-specific ways, which limits their use in other domains. This paper introduces Subset Acquisition with Learned Value Estimates and Search (SALVES), a framework that decomposes subset selection into two components. First, a value model is trained by supervised learning on tasks where the hidden information is known. On a new task, it predicts the utility each candidate would add to the current selection. Second, a selection step chooses the subset from these predictions, typically by simulated annealing with a diversity term penalising redundancy. The value model transfers to new classes, pretrained networks, datasets and sensors, and from synthetic to real data. On the four applications, SALVES matches or outperforms application-specific baselines on average. It requires substantially fewer bands for equal accuracy and remains reliable in input selection where individual baselines fail.
